articles.title: 👾 Nested Bookmarks Organizer for Chrome w/Custom Ticker
articles.description: ✨ Finally, some positive excitement! ✨  I went on a tiny mission last night to build something I...
articles.body_html:
✨ Finally, some positive excitement! ✨

I went on a tiny mission last night to build something I wanted for myself. I was inspired by seeing a space theme on someone's browser in a tutorial and thinking, "I am a developer, I want a cool browser!"

🔎 What I Found

It just so happens that space is generally my favorite theme. Feeling inspired, I found a cool theme in the chrome store. I generally avoid extensions but was feeling strongly about this one.

Between Google chromes sidebar/group coloring and the space background, I was starting to feel more at home. But that was just the beginning.

👷‍♀️ What I Did

Then I remembered my chaotic array of bookmarks. I really wanted to manage them better, with nested folders and groups, as is the tried and true method in general. There were a few options available on the chrome webstore, but nothing that was truly motivating.

I wanted to hold onto a space/cyberpunk theme so I would love it. Using Claude Opus 5.5 I was able to get the extension loaded and bookmarks organized quickly. I was shocked at the sheer speed I was able to pull this off. Within that same time frame, I realized I had gained a tremendous amount of space at the bottom of my bookmarks organizer. What is this foreign land? 😂 I thought to myself It would be really cool if I had a ticker with updates from sources that matter to me.

Connecting Ticker Feeds

  • I had Claude pull data from DEV from my notifications, and the same method 'unofficially' works for linked in.
  • I added a server activity ticker. I had already implemented a traffic analysis tool prior, building off of Goaccess server logs and fail2ban. So this was an easy setup. That being the case I still learned about symlink (symbolic links) which is a special pointer that references another drive or partition on another device. So cool! I always wanted that! 😂 So I fed my server notifications to my browser ticker with a symlink.
  • To see recent sales on my store, I simply integrated stripe with a heavily restricted API key. This helps ensure I can act quickly for a customer. This pairs well with my discord notification bot. I am usually in my browser or in discord, so no excuses! 😂

Originally a tabbed interface, I switched it to a stacked layer view so I can see updates in real time with a glance. I LOVE that.

Beautifully nested folders in a cyberpunk UI with drag-and-drop and label editing, a personalized ticker, and a space background! I am feeling much more in the element and overall please with the situation. I will undoubtedly add more tickers for interesting things as I go through time. But this is a fabulous improvement.

What cool browser creations have you made? Please share below!

I have a template repo up for anyone that might be interested. (If you find it useful could you leave me a star? 😂)

I made sure I templated the project this time and added an MIT license. I think I covered everything this time? +1 XP? 🤣

AnnaVi11arrea1 / cyber-bookmarks

A much cooler way to keep track of the information you deem important right in the chrome browser.

NEURAL//LINKS — Cyberpunk Bookmarks

A neon side-panel bookmark manager for Chrome, with an optional Signal Feed that pulls in your LinkedIn and dev.to notifications, Stripe sales, and security alerts from your own Linux server.

Features

  • Bookmarks in the side panel. Drag to reorder, drop onto a folder to nest it, and group items into folders with Ctrl/Shift+click and then ⧉ GROUP (Ctrl+G). Right-click an item for more options.
  • Full-screen view. Click ⤢ to open the same tree in a tab.
  • Signal Feed. It checks every 5 minutes and shows new items as a badge count on the toolbar icon. It can also send desktop alerts.
  • Your real bookmarks. It edits Chrome's own bookmarks, so changes sync wherever Chrome sync does.

Install the extension

  1. Download or clone this repo.
  2. Open chrome://extensions and turn on Developer mode (top right).
  3. Click Load unpacked and select the project folder (the one with manifest.json).
  4. …
View on GitHub

Generally, to get this effect, I had to build on top of Googles pre-existing bookmarks since that cannot be changed. So this bookmarks interface is an extension that build on top of what already exists - not a replacement. This is a solid way to manage things in a lightweight manner.

Space Explorer Mode: Activated! 👾⚡

articles.title: Day 22 of Building Crowdwide: I Thought UI Polish Would Be Easy, BUT I WAS WRONGGGGG 😭
articles.description: I was building the social media platform for newly created creators and someone who wants a simple...
articles.body_html:
I was building the social media platform for newly created creators and someone who wants a simple place to post and make a community or indie page for growing. Crowdwide has an algorithm for that, which shows posts and things according to the interests of the user, and with its design, new people in a larger community get a chance to grow faster!!

The current state of Crowdwide is quite interesting.

I'm done with all its core features, and now it's time to just polish the UI and make it clearer, cleaner, and more authentic!

And I thought it would be a simple, easy task! What do I need to do? Just change the color and give it a few more CSS properties!!

BUT I WAS WRONGGGGG... 😭

I was deeply checking the UI of Crowdwide and found some places where margin was required, some places where padding was required, and some places where border-radius was destroying the look of the page (profile page).

After noting everything down, I found a few more things to change.

@effessdev suggested me to add optimistic UI.

I never thought this was an important part because if the server is working, it will hardly take 1–2 seconds to update, so I always ignored this thing. And in Crowdwide, I never thought that I should implement this, and wasn't expecting this as a suggestion too!!

But thanks, EffessDev, for pointing this out, and now I just fixed this too!!

And for UI and layout improvement, I was so confused. Odinaka Robert Nnamani, Rosana, and Oleksandr helped me and gave great suggestions!

So I have changed the sidebar, like made it separate from the layer of the feed. Now it opens and closes, and when it opens, the background gets blurred and a little dimmer, so it gets focused!

And I thought I should remove the gradient background, and now it feels good. But still, I kept that gradient background in some places, not removed completely from the platform.

and now UI looks something like this...:

And Crowdwide got:

13 members

65 posts shared

4 communities

And this is a shoutout to the top members of Crowdwide.

Thanks for the suggestions!!
comment if you think anything is left...

Links:

🌐 Live platform: https://www.crowdwide.run.place/

💻 GitHub repository: https://github.com/DeveloperPuneet/Crowdwide

articles.title: I turned my portfolio into a playground (plug a theme into a display to open it)
articles.description: My portfolio has three versions now. To switch between them I built Theme Studio, a small canvas where you drag a wire into a display.
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone 👋

Last time I shared my rebuilt portfolio with a terminal theme. It has a third theme now (a notebook one), and I built a small playground just to switch between them 😄

Meet Theme Studio → mahmad.me/theme-studio

How it works

The three versions of my site are cards on a canvas, with a display in the middle. To open one, you drag a wire from its card into the display, like plugging a cable into an old TV. 🔌

The fun parts

  • ⚡ Lightning sparks jump between the wire and the display when you get close.
  • 📦 Skill icons ride down the wire once it's plugged in.
  • 📺 The screen turns on like an old TV, and then the page opens.

Fast navigation from every page

I didn't want people to hunt for the playground, so a small live copy of it sits in the bottom-right corner of the home page, the terminal theme and the notebook theme (on desktop). It plugs in one theme after another, and one click opens the real thing.

Source code

MA-Ahmad / myPortfolio

A pixel-perfect portfolio with three themes and a Theme Studio playground

My personal portfolio, showing my skills, experience, projects and articles. It also has a playground where you can switch between three versions of the site.

→ Live site: mahmad.me















Home page · mahmad.me


Playground · mahmad.me/theme-studio



Notebook theme · mahmad.me/themes/notebook


Terminal theme · mahmad.me/themes/terminal

Overview

Stack

  • Next.js 16 and React 19
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Framer Motion
  • Prisma with PostgreSQL
  • Cloudflare Workers

Featured

  • Light/Dark themes
  • Three versions of the site: classic, terminal and notebook
  • Playground: Theme Studio, where you drag a wire from a theme into a display to open it, with live cursors from other visitors
  • Blog from local MDX posts and Dev.to articles
  • GitHub contribution graph
  • Command menu (⌘ K)
  • AI-ready with /llms.txt
  • Link preview image for sharing

License

Everything in this repository is licensed under the MIT license.

If you fork it, make sure to remove all my personal information (profile, projects, blog posts…


View on GitHub


If you like it, a star ⭐ really helps. What should I plug into the display next? Tell me in the comments 👇

articles.title: Let It Die: The Lazy Email Agent on TabPFN, Gemma and Temporal
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Most “lazy” agents do your chores faster. Let It Die asks whether the chore needs doing at all.

It reads incoming email and scores each message on how likely it is that ignoring it would cost you something. Then it does one of three things:

  • Need you (top 20% by score): a local Gemma model writes a two-line summary and a suggested action for a morning digest.
  • Low priority (middle 60%): left alone and counted in the digest.
  • Let it die (bottom 20%): parked on a durable Temporal timer. If the sender follows up within 7 days, the email is escalated. If nothing arrives, it is archived.

Anyone whose inbox is full of mail that sorts itself out gets to be a little lazier: the cheapest task to finish is the one you never started, as long as you can tell which ones those are. On my held-out test slice of 1,981 emails, 398 (20%) were parked, and about 85% of them really got no reply.

Demo

Real output from a run on held-out email:

397 need you | 1186 low-priority | 398 parked on a timer (let it die)
In the 'need you' bucket, 46% were actually replied to (overall: 30%)

- john.henderson@enron.com | Wharton Tm #3 Presentation | he replied
  Summary: John reviewed the Wharton Tm #3 presentation and found it to be a good start.

In the parking demo, 8 emails were picked at random from the let-it-die bucket. 7 were archived, and all 7 truly needed no reply. 1 was escalated, because the sender wrote again.

Code

Khushighosh / let-it-die

Let It Die: an agent whose main skill is deciding not to act

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3 ("Slow and Steady").

Most "lazy" agents do your chores faster. This one asks whether the chore needs doing at all. It scores each incoming email on how likely ignoring it is to cost you something, then:

  • Need you (top 20% by score): a local Gemma model writes a two-line summary and a suggested action for the morning digest.
  • Low priority (middle 60%): left alone, counted in the digest.
  • Let it die (bottom 20%): parked on a durable Temporal timer. If the sender follows up within 7 days, the email is escalated. If nothing arrives, it is archived.
emails ──> TabPFN score ──> triage ──┬─ need you ──> Gemma summary ──> morning digest
                                     ├─ low priority ──> counted only
                                     └─ let it die ──> Temporal timer (7 days)
                                                         ├─
…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. The README has the run steps (Windows, Python 3.12).

How I Built It 

emails -> TabPFN score -> triage -+- need you -> Gemma summary -> morning digest
                                  +- low priority -> counted only
                                  +- let it die -> Temporal timer (7 days)
                                                    +- follow-up signal -> escalate
                                                    +- timeout -> archive
  • TabPFN (Prior Labs) predicts whether the owner replied within 7 days, from features built only from information available before each email arrived: sender history, who it was addressed to, time of day, subject and body cues, thread length. It needs no training run.
  • Gemma (gemma3:4b through Ollama, running locally) writes the summaries and suggested actions for the need-you bucket.
  • Temporal runs one workflow per parked email. It waits for either a follow-up signal or a 7-day timeout, then escalates or archives. My demo uses Temporal’s time-skipping test server, so a week of waiting runs in seconds. When I made the first archive attempt fail on purpose, Temporal retried every one automatically, and all 7 archived emails logged attempt 2.
  • Sentry traces the whole run: the agent, the triage step, each Gemma call (model, token counts, full prompt and response) and the Temporal step. About 22 of the 23 seconds were the five local Gemma calls, each with an HTTP call to 127.0.0.1, my own machine. Triage took about a millisecond and parking eight emails about 1.3 seconds.

The data. I don’t have a two-sided mailbox of my own, so I used one mailbox of about 28,000 messages from the public Enron corpus (CMU, May 2015 release), which includes sent folders and lets me derive reply labels. The label is “the owner replied in the same thread within 7 days.” Sent mail stops being archived after May 2001, so every later email would look unanswered; I cut the timeline to Nov 1999 through May 2001, which left 9,902 usable emails. I trained on the earliest 80% (7,921 emails) and tested on the latest 20% (1,981 emails, 70.5% of which got no reply). The split is by time, so the model never sees the future.

Model ROC AUC Ignore lowest 10%: truly no reply / replied-to mail missed Ignore lowest 20%
Sender reply-rate rule 0.579 68.2% / 10.8% 73.7% / 17.8%
Gradient boosting 0.662 92.4% / 2.6% 88.4% / 7.9%
TabPFN 0.687 92.9% / 2.4% 84.6% / 10.4%

What I take from it:

  • Both models clearly beat a rule based on the sender’s past reply rate.
  • TabPFN’s AUC is higher by 0.024 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.003 to 0.043), but gradient boosting wins the 20% bucket. I call them comparable.
  • The practical headline: the agent can park about 1 in 10 emails and be right 92 to 93% of the time, missing about 2.5% of the mail that actually got a reply.
  • In the test slice, the need-you bucket was replied to 46% of the time against 30% overall, and the let-it-die bucket about 15%. It is a prioritizer, not an oracle.

What went wrong, and how I found it

  • Every file looked missing. Enron filenames end in a dot (1., 10.), and Windows quietly strips it, so Python saw an empty mailbox until I switched to Windows’ extended-length path prefix.
  • The first test set had no positives. The model scored a meaningless 98% accuracy. A month-by-month table showed replies falling to exactly 0 from June 2001, because the archive stops containing sent mail. I cut the timeline there.
  • Gemma summarized the wrong message. For an email where the sender wrote one line on top of a long forwarded chain, the summary described the oldest forwarded message. I found it by reading the cached email text next to the summary. Cutting each email at the first forwarded-message marker fixed that case: over five runs each (the last two of each at temperature 0 with a fixed seed), the unfixed version summarized the forwarded message every time and the fixed version summarized the sender’s reply every time. The prompt for that email also shrank from 649 to 90 tokens.

Limitations

  • “Replied within 7 days” is only a proxy for “needed action,” and “the sender wrote again” is a noisy follow-up signal. One escalated email in my demo came from a mailing list that re-sent the same subject line.
  • One mailbox, one time-based split. The bootstrap interval treats emails as independent, though threads and senders cluster, so it is probably a little too tight.
  • The parking demo uses 8 emails and a simulated clock, and “archive” writes to a log file instead of moving real mail.
  • Gemma output is not deterministic, and identical prompts varied about 2x in latency between runs, so I only quote token counts for the forwarded-chain fix. That fix is one email, not a benchmark, and suggested actions vary between runs.
  • Attachments aren’t in the email text, so suggested actions for attachment-only emails are generic.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The model that reads my mail runs on my machine. Gemma runs locally through Ollama, and the Sentry trace shows every model call going to 127.0.0.1. There is no API bill and no third party reading the text.
  • The waiting is durable and I don’t run a scheduler. Temporal’s open-source tooling gave me timers that survive restarts and retries for flaky steps, with no cron job or home-made queue.
  • No training run. TabPFN fits a small personal mailbox without a training step. The honest caveat: I used the hosted API, so the 5,000 training rows went to Prior Labs’ servers. I only did that with the public Enron data, and a deployment on private mail would need local weights or to accept that tradeoff.
  • Anyone can reproduce the numbers. The data is public and the code is in the repo.

I didn’t test a hosted LLM, so I can’t claim open wins on summary quality. The case for open here is privacy, cost and not depending on a service staying up.

The Lazy Payoff

I haven’t pointed it at my own inbox, because I don’t have a two-sided mailbox, so these numbers come from public Enron mail, not from my own week. On the held-out slice of 1,981 emails, the agent would have taken 398 (20%) off the owner’s plate, and about 85% of those really got no reply. The price is the other 15%, about 60 emails that did get a reply and would have been archived unless the sender nudged again, which is about 10% of all the mail that was replied to. Each summary takes about 4 seconds on my laptop. I can’t honestly put a number on minutes saved, so I’m not going to.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of TabPFN: the ignore-or-act predictor, compared with a rule and gradient boosting, with a bootstrap interval on the difference.
  • Best Use of Gemma: local gemma3:4b summaries and suggested actions, with a documented failure and fix.
  • Best Use of Temporal: one durable workflow per parked email, with a follow-up signal, a 7-day timeout and automatic retries.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: a trace of the whole run with token counts, prompts and responses, and the before and after of the forwarded-chain fix.

articles.title: 👻 The $249 Ghost Sale
articles.description: Before I get into it, I just want to say that my recent unemployment has left me a vast amount of...
articles.body_html:
Before I get into it, I just want to say that my recent unemployment has left me a vast amount of tinkering time, which I very much enjoy. I have so much unfinished business and projects, I'm not even sure that I want to actively look for work right now. 😅 It is absolutely amazing to have some free time to work on things! I consider myself lucky to be in a position at the moment where I can (sort of 😅) afford to take a brief break from the working world.

You know when you are working full time and doing all that life demands of you, it's nearly impossible to fully immerse your self in a bunch of little visions that sprout in your brain. You may try, but it's simply not the same as a full on investment. You start projects, have ideas, grand plans even. You start them, you get distracted, and they get placed on the back burner and fade into the sands of time. dramatic ethereal sounds

Not this woman and not at this moment! 👻 So let's get to it, the ghost sales.

1. The Hat

I asked claude to put on it's google analytics hat. Yes, I actually told it that. I sell blacklight reactive art, tapestries, and clothing. The designs come from my own paintings or graphic art. I recently built a Rails shop for it and run it on a tiny server at home. Sales were seriously lacking and I wanted to know what the best move was so I could get a few more sales.

I connected my analytics and ad accounts to claude and asked the question: "given the historical data, what should I do?

2. Confident Wrong Answers

  • First Idea: Purchase tracking was broken because my Google Analytics tag lived on my old Shopify store. Wrong, the tag was on my real site, and was sending ecommerce events for weeks.
  • Second Idea: My ads were sending people to the dead Shopify store. They were not, the ads pointed to the right place the whole time.

After these ideas were checked off the list, claude ran some checking of hostnames, page sources, and the actual code. This produced some monumental findings.

3. A customer placed a large order, and Google never saw it

Google analytics was showing ZERO purchases, ever. I knew with my own eyes, discord alert bot, stripe dashboard, and bank account that this transaction did indeed happen. Someone had placed an order for about $249.

😅 So for as long as this store has existed, Google Ads had been trying to find more buyers without ever being told what a buyer looked like. It was instead optimizing for add to carts, which, in October, also numbered zero.

Here is my October: 675 visits 29 product views, and 0 add-to-carts. Claude stated exactly:

"People walked in, looked at the homepage like it was a museum lobby, and left."

My art can't possibly be that terrible. 😂😂😂 Without letting it eat away at my ego, I knew that I had unfinished business with Google Analytics, and that this storm was bound to happen. So I braced for the impending doom.

4. The Ads: 2 Accounts, one was empty

Of my two Google Ads accounts, one had all the history. The other had nothing at all, just vibing out in the Google Analytics cosmos. 🕶️

5. Graveyard of dead links 🪦

I've been selling online for years. The Shopify and Etsy links were still out in the wild wreaking havoc on my ads performance.

This included:

  • Facebook Posts
  • Google results
  • a dev.to article
  • Instagram
  • Snapchat

Analytics logged 155 different old paths getting visits, each resulting in a 404. dies, rolls over, and dies a second time

--> Side Tangent: You can connect claude to supermetrics and use a free trial. That was a saving grace for someone new to Google Analytics. Highly recommend, they have a free trial!

Claude built me a redirect map with 191 entries. Old products go to their new pages. A retired bikini goes to a search for bikinis. Old policy goes to new policy. Every link was checked against the live site.

click http://shop.everfluorescent.art/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie-mens-fleece-full-zip-hoodie-model-h60
301   https://www.everfluorescent.com/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie-mens-fleece-full-zip-hoodie-model-h60
301   https://www.everfluorescent.com/products/winged-cat-fleece-hoodie
200   a hoodie, at last

I had to make a detour to the domain registrar. The first forwards were 'temporary' and 'don't include the path,' so all the old links landed on the homepage. Back to the museum lobby. Then I discovered an expired SSL certificate which expired on October 9th. It's supposed to be renewing at the moment. 😂

6. Production running a feature branch, and other confessions

I'm just going to drop a screenshot, the artifact frames it beautifully.

...in my defense the aftermath of having too much unfinished business! 😅🤣

End of Day Summary 10/24/2026

Metric Result
Old links that now go somewhere 191
Products ready for Google Shopping 340 items
Purchases Google can now actually see All of them
Ad campaigns I paused by accident 2
Confidently wrong diagnoses 2
Commands I typed that the AI didn't suggest, which worked 1
Mystery ad accounts still at large Maybe 1

No guilt or shame, just slight embarrassment.

I have only myself to answer to. I have definitely wasted money. All the more reason to hold myself accountable for fixing it. I guess I didn't realize how wild I made things, having Etsy shops and Shopify's from 2019. You have to clean up all your old stuff. The big lesson here I learned is just that. I spent so much time trying to create a brand presence online that I polluted the web with broken links and old paths.

That very behavior was sending potential customers to repeated 404 pages, and for that, I feel slightly unnerved albeit comedic for the reader. This is me being as transparent as possible in my journey.

If you recently visited one of my links and got a 404 I would encourage you to try again, and let me know how bad my work is tomorrow. 🤣 Thanks for reading my drama, everyone.

** I used snippets of an artifact I had Claude create for me after this experience to help me write this post. Some things were re-written from the artifact and somethings are my own unique thoughts.

articles.title: You know you can automate screen reader tests right?
articles.description: There is a common misconception that accessibility testing can only fall into two groups:   Some...
articles.body_html:
There is a common misconception that accessibility testing can only fall into two groups:

  1. Some limited amount of static analysis performed by something like Axe
  2. Manual testing for everything else, either by yourself, your tester, your AI agent(?), your resident accessibility expert, or hopefully real assistive technology users

If you've gone a step further, you might even have some coverage in your functional test suite of choice for keyboard interactions (most cool!), but have you ever considered that you could also be testing with some popular screen reader technologies as well?

Instead of querying the DOM to find a button, or checking its accessible name from the browser's internal accessibility tree, you could be navigating using a real screen reader and assert against what it actually announces.

In this post we'll walk you through how to set it up with Guidepup running against the BBC Homepage - spoiler alert, it's two extra CLI commands and then whatever tests you fancy writing!

Getting started

For this walkthrough we're going to use Playwright, but you can bring your own testing library of choice!

The first step to screen reader automation is to configure your machine, which can be done in one command:

# Add the --ci flag if running in CI!
npx @guidepup/setup

Then in your project directory install your test dependencies as you would usually, but with a few extra Guidepup packages that will be handling the screen reader automation:

# If you're not using Playwright then drop the last package!
npm i @playwright/test @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright

Then as you would normally, install your Playwright browser(s) of choice - for this walkthrough we'll stick to WebKit:

npx playwright install webkit

And for the last "extra" step vs a standard Playwright project setup, we run the following command to install our screen reader assets - basically the equivalent to the Playwright command we just ran, but for screen readers instead of browsers!

npx @guidepup/setup install

Setup done! 🎉

Playwright config

We need this anyway, the only difference is we wrap our config in a withGuidepup() utility:

// playwright.config.ts
import { devices } from "@playwright/test";
import { withGuidepup } from "@guidepup/playwright";

const config = withGuidepup({
  projects: [
    {
      name: "webkit",
      use: { ...devices["Desktop Safari"] },
    },
  ],
});

export default config;

If you're introducing this to an existing test suite you can also create this as a separate playwright.guidepup-config.ts or similar.

This wrapper makes sure that the Playwright test runs are always headed as screen readers cannot operate against headless browsers.

Playwright test

Last step! Let's dive straight in with the pertinent code:

// bbc.test.ts

// We import our test instance from Guidepup's Playwright package -
// it's the same as the Playwright test version but with a
// `screenReader` instance available, a bit like the `page`
// instance
import { screenReaderTest as test } from "@guidepup/playwright";
import { expect } from "@playwright/test";

const MAX_NAVIGATION = 100;

const log = (...messages: string[]) =>
  console.log(`[${new Date().toUTCString()}]`, ...messages);

test.describe("BBC screen reader tests", () => {
  test.beforeEach(
    async ({ context, page, screenReader }) => {
      // Skip the pesky cookie banner.
      await context.addCookies([
        {
          name: "ckns_explicit",
          value: "1",
          domain: "www.bbc.co.uk",
          path: "/",
        },
      ]);

      // Prevent the BBC redirecting us to their international site.
      await page.route("https://www.bbc.co.uk/userinfo**", (route) =>
        route.abort(),
      );

      // Navigate to our target page.
      await page.goto("https://www.bbc.co.uk/", {
        waitUntil: "load",
      });

      // Wait for the page to load.
      await page.locator("header").waitFor();

      // Navigate the screen reader to the web content!!
      await screenReader.navigateToWebContent();

      // That's us now at the beginning of the web page
      // with our screen reader :o
    },
  );

  test("I can navigate to BBC Sounds using a screen reader", async ({
    screenReader,
  }) => {
    let lastSpokenPhrase = "";
    let navigationCounter = 0;

    // Let's navigate to their "More menu" button on the
    // site header.
    while (!/More menu/i.test(lastSpokenPhrase)) {
      if (navigationCounter >= MAX_NAVIGATION) {
        throw new Error("Failed to find 'More menu' button");
      }

      // Navigate to the next item with the screen reader.
      // For VoiceOver this does "VO+Right Arrow", for NVDA this
      // does "Right Arrow", for Orca this does
      // "Orca+Ctrl+Right Arrow".
      await screenReader.next();
      lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
      log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

      navigationCounter++;
    }

    // Activate the control under the screen reader cursor, usually
    // similar to keying "Enter" with a keyboard.
    // This is so we can expand the menu to find BBC Sounds!
    await screenReader.act();
    lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
    log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

    navigationCounter = 0;

    // And finally, continue our search for the desired link.
    while (!/Sounds/i.test(lastSpokenPhrase)) {
      if (navigationCounter >= MAX_NAVIGATION) {
        throw new Error("Failed to find 'Sounds' link");
      }

      await screenReader.next();
      lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
      log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

      navigationCounter++;
    }

    // We're here, visit the link!
    await screenReader.act();
    lastSpokenPhrase = await screenReader.lastSpokenPhrase();
    log(`Last spoken phrase: ${lastSpokenPhrase}`);

    // Let's assert that we actually got to BBC Sounds!
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/bbc\.co\.uk\/sounds/);

    // And finally log out the entire journey - in your tests this
    // could be assertions or even a snapshot.
    log(
      `Spoken phrase log: ${JSON.stringify(
        await screenReader.spokenPhraseLog(),
      )}`,
    );
  });
});

Not working for you? I don't own the website so it could have changed! Please also be considerate when testing against sites you don't own!

Follow along ok? 😅

The key bits are:

  1. Import your test instance from @guidepup/playwright not @playwright/test to get access to the generic screenReader instance, or voiceOver, nvda, or orca instances if targeting a specific screen reader.
  2. Once your page is loaded, use the screenReader.navigateToWebContent() command to land on the web content.
  3. Make use of screenReader commands to navigate through the page and assert on what was spoken through the screen reader.

This test is basic - we're mostly using next, act and lastSpokenPhrase, but Guidepup also supports the full command set for VoiceOver, NVDA, and Orca, so you can go wild with more realistic journeys, e.g. navigating by headings, landmarks, and links.

For your own tests you can probably drop some of the log() logic, it's there so I can easily dump the output for this post 😄 - talking of which here's the log output from a macos-latest GitHub actions run (which automatically uses VoiceOver):

What's next

  • Start with your static analysis tests such as Axe for a base level
  • Have a think about what critical user journeys you have
  • Test them out manually with some key OS + browser + screen reader combos
  • Fix any issues
  • Then convert your manual test to Guidepup based tests to cover you from future regressions!

Same as mouse and keyboard regression tests, you can't test everything, but a small set of golden path tests for your core features can go a long way to ensuring your site can work for screen reader users!

The real benefit here is catching accessibility regressions before they reach your users. Once you've manually tested a critical user journey and automated it with Guidepup, you can run it as part of your existing test suite every time you make a change. If a button's announcement changes, a link becomes harder to find, or a journey stops working as expected, your tests can flag it before it ships.

Think you want to go further? With the dawn of Agentic AI I am curious what level of exploratory and/or chaos testing you can achieve to battle test a site? Maybe give it a go and report back? 😉

articles.title: Add On-Device Summarization to React with Chrome's Summarizer API
articles.description: A travel brief often mixes the trip itself with meeting context, preferences, and unresolved...
articles.body_html:
A travel brief often mixes the trip itself with meeting context, preferences, and unresolved decisions. A short summary can help the person review it before requesting proposed form changes.

That is a useful place for Chrome’s Summarizer API: a bounded reading aid beside an existing text field.

In Trip Workbench, the public demo I built and maintain, the original brief already feeds a separate Gemini feature that proposes trip fields for review. The local summary has a different purpose. It helps the person read the brief; it does not update the trip, replace the source text, or decide which details the cloud model receives.

This walkthrough builds on commit 4b3f370. The demo has the basic API call. The lifecycle extensions below add capability states, download feedback, cancellation, and a boundary that prevents an old summary from appearing beside a changed brief.

Choose a reading task with a clear boundary

Consider this synthetic brief:

I need to attend a customer workshop in New York on November 12–13, 2026. Depart SFO for JFK on November 11. Economy, one traveler. Do not book a hotel because I will stay with family. Travel only if the client confirms the workshop by Friday. Plan to return November 14, but November 15 is still possible if the workshop extends.

A useful summary would preserve the dates, the hotel exclusion, the confirmation condition, and the uncertainty around the return. A fluent summary that converts those details into a confirmed itinerary would be misleading.

Keep the original visible beside the output. Label the result “Summary of this brief” and let the person regenerate it after editing.

Continue sending the original brief to Gemini when the person selects “Suggest trip details.” Using a lossy summary as the extraction input would make any omitted condition harder for the next step to recover.

The feature needs no application API key or @google/genai call. Chrome supplies the on-device model. Chrome documents that model use does not send the input to Google or a third party, while initial model setup can require a download. That statement applies to the local inference path; the application’s separate Gemini request remains a cloud operation. See Chrome’s Summarizer guide.

Treat availability as part of the interface

Chrome documents Summarizer support from version 138, subject to platform, hardware, storage, and model availability. It remains a limited-availability web API, so browser version alone is insufficient. Serve the feature in a secure context and retain the ordinary text workflow.

There are two checks: whether the API exists, and whether it can support the configuration you want.

Use the same core options for checking availability and creating the instance. This example requests English key points in plain text. The existing demo uses a short tldr; medium key points give this review task more room without guaranteeing that every detail survives.

The examples use JavaScript and JSX. For TypeScript, Chrome recommends @types/dom-chromium-ai. Replace the demo’s handwritten Summarizer global declaration if adopting those types.

In summary-client.js:

export const summaryOptions = {
  type: "key-points",
  format: "plain-text",
  length: "medium",
  expectedInputLanguages: ["en"],
  outputLanguage: "en",
};

export async function checkSummaryAvailability(API = globalThis.Summarizer) {
  if (!API) return "unsupported";
  try {
    const value = await API.availability(summaryOptions);
    return ["available", "downloadable", "downloading", "unavailable"].includes(value)
      ? value : "unknown";
  } catch {
    return "error";
  }
}

Map the availability result to a useful UI state:

State What the interface should do
Checking Keep the brief editable while checking support
Unsupported or unavailable Explain that on-device summarization cannot run here
Downloadable Offer the action and explain that model setup may require a download
Downloading Offer to wait for readiness and show progress once attached
Available Offer summarization immediately
Unknown or error Offer a readiness retry and preserve the brief

Run this capability check in a parent Effect with a cleanup guard so a late result cannot update an abandoned panel. Do not call create() from that Effect.

Chrome’s setup guidance requires user interaction when model downloads are needed. Let the Summarize button call creation directly. Separating the readiness probe also keeps a potentially slow check out of the click path.

Availability can change. A successful probe is not a reservation; creation still needs error handling. When the language or summary configuration changes, check the new options again.

Own the summarizer for one request

For this occasional button action, one instance per request keeps resource ownership straightforward. Create it, generate the summary, and release it in finally.

Add this function to the same module:

export async function summarizeBrief(
  brief,
  { signal, onUpdate = () => {} },
  API = globalThis.Summarizer,
) {
  signal.throwIfAborted();
  if (!API) throw new Error("On-device summarization is unavailable.");
  if (!brief.trim()) throw new Error("Enter a brief first.");

  let session;
  try {
    session = await API.create({
      ...summaryOptions,
      signal,
      monitor(monitor) {
        monitor.addEventListener("downloadprogress", event => {
          if (!signal.aborted) onUpdate({
            phase: "downloading",
            percent: Math.round(event.loaded * 100),
          });
        }, { signal });
      },
    });
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    onUpdate({ phase: "summarizing" });
    const text = await session.summarize(brief, { signal });
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    return text;
  } finally {
    session?.destroy();
  }
}

The signal goes to both create() and summarize(). Cancelling while creation is pending must reach that operation, too. Aborting a creation signal after it resolves also destroys the resulting instance, so this signal belongs to this one request.

The final abort check prevents a late result from being accepted after cancellation. The finally block releases any instance that was acquired, including when generation fails.

Download progress and generation are separate phases. The Writing Assistance API specification defines download progress as a fraction with a total of 1. A displayed 100% means the download stage reached completion; the interface should still wait for instance creation and summarization to finish.

Destroying an instance releases its resources. It does not mean that the browser removes its downloaded model, nor does this code promise to cancel a shared download for every other page.

Batch output keeps this first implementation small. Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness for longer output, but it also requires managing incomplete text and clearing partial results when the request becomes stale.

Bind the result to the brief that produced it

The current demo creates an AbortController inside its click handler but does not retain it for cancellation. It also stores the resulting text without binding it to a brief version.

A person can therefore edit the brief while a summary is running, or start another request before the first finishes. The last response to arrive can overwrite the display even when it belongs to older input.

A dedicated summary component can own one active controller. This hook cancels earlier work and accepts updates only from the currently active request:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { summarizeBrief } from "./summary-client.js";

export function useBriefSummary(brief) {
  const active = useRef(null);
  const [view, setView] = useState({ phase: "idle" });

  useEffect(() => () => {
    active.current?.abort();
    active.current = null;
  }, []);

  function cancel() {
    active.current?.abort();
    active.current = null;
    setView({ phase: "cancelled" });
  }

  async function start() {
    active.current?.abort();
    const controller = new AbortController();
    active.current = controller;
    const isCurrent = () =>
      active.current === controller && !controller.signal.aborted;

    setView({ phase: "preparing" });
    try {
      const text = await summarizeBrief(brief, {
        signal: controller.signal,
        onUpdate(update) {
          if (isCurrent()) setView(update);
        },
      });
      if (isCurrent()) setView({ phase: "done", text });
    } catch (error) {
      if (active.current !== controller) return;
      setView({
        phase: controller.signal.aborted ? "cancelled" : "error",
        message: error?.name === "QuotaExceededError"
          ? "This brief is too long. Choose a smaller section."
          : "Could not summarize on this device. Try again or keep reading the brief.",
      });
    } finally {
      if (active.current === controller) active.current = null;
    }
  }

  return { view, start, cancel };
}

The hook controls request ordering within one mounted summary component. Bind that component’s identity to the source so an edit also clears an already completed summary.

Trip Workbench already tracks briefVersion, editor generation, and session generation. Use them with the draft ID:

const summarySourceKey = JSON.stringify([
  state.sessionGeneration,
  state.editorGeneration,
  state.savedDraft?.id,
  state.briefVersion,
]);

<BriefSummary
  key={summarySourceKey}
  brief={state.brief}
  readiness={readiness}
/>

React resets component state when its key changes. That removes the previous output, and the hook’s cleanup aborts its request. Keep the textarea in the parent so typing retains focus.

Using the existing brief version also invalidates a result when the person edits and then restores the same text. If summary options become editable, include their version in this identity as well.

The availability probe can stay in the parent, since changing the brief does not change this example’s fixed language configuration.

Show useful states and preserve the source

Inside BriefSummary, call the hook and derive whether work is in progress:

const { view, start, cancel } = useBriefSummary(brief);
const busy = ["preparing", "downloading", "summarizing"].includes(view.phase);
const canRun = ["available", "downloadable", "downloading"].includes(readiness);

return (
  <section aria-label="Brief summary">
    <button
      type="button"
      disabled={!canRun || busy || !brief.trim()}
      onClick={() => void start()}
    >
      Summarize on this device
    </button>
    {busy && <button type="button" onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>}
    <p role="status">
      {view.phase === "preparing" && "Preparing on-device summarization…"}
      {view.phase === "downloading" && `Downloading model: ${view.percent}%`}
      {view.phase === "summarizing" && "Summarizing…"}
      {view.phase === "cancelled" && "Summary cancelled."}
      {view.phase === "done" && "Summary ready."}
      {view.phase === "error" && view.message}
    </p>
    {view.phase === "done" && (
      <>
        <h3>Summary of this brief</h3>
        <p style={{ whiteSpace: "pre-wrap" }}>{view.text}</p>
        <p>Generated on this device. Check details against the original brief.</p>
      </>
    )}
  </section>
);

Place the readiness explanation and a readiness-retry button beside this control in the parent. A disabled action should have a reason the person can read.

Render the plain-text result through React text interpolation. The summary does not need HTML insertion.

Long inputs can exceed the model’s input quota. The summarize() API can reject with QuotaExceededError; the hook turns that into a request to choose a smaller section. For a document-oriented feature, measureInputUsage() and inputQuota can support an earlier check. A character count is not an exact token or quota measurement.

The fallback remains useful: the person can read and edit the original brief, then use the rest of the form. A cloud summary could be a separate action with a clear explanation that it sends the text to a server. Failure of the local path should not silently trigger that transfer.

Test lifecycle behavior and summary quality separately

The existing Summarizer unit test checks the missing-API case. That is a useful start, but it does not establish behavior during downloads, cancellation, or editing.

For the adapter shown here, eight controlled checks pass with a fake Summarizer. They cover availability states, availability errors, cancellation before creation, immediate creation in the call path, cancellation during creation, progress and input forwarding, rejected late output, and cleanup after generation errors.

These are lifecycle results. The React wiring has not been mounted in a browser during this walkthrough, and no native model output or performance measurement is claimed.

Use component tests for replacement requests, brief changes, draft changes, unmounting, and Strict Mode cleanup. Assert that an old result never appears beside a new source. Keep those tests deterministic with deferred promises.

Then run native browser checks with a small set of briefs:

Case What to inspect
First use on a supported device Readiness, download feedback, cancellation, and eventual completion
Model already ready Creation and generation latency without mixing in first-download time
Brief edited during generation Old output disappears and cannot return
Unsupported configuration A clear explanation and an intact editing workflow
Long brief A recoverable quota response with the original text retained
Travel brief above Dates, negation, conditions, and uncertainty preserved without invented commitments

For the travel brief, record whether the output preserves “do not book a hotel,” the client-confirmation condition, and the uncertain return date. These are evaluation criteria, not recorded model results.

Measure correctness alongside usefulness: how long it takes the person to review the summary and source, how often important details are omitted, and whether the summary saves effort at all. Very short briefs may be faster to read directly.

This gives the feature a clear role in the wider assistant: a local reading aid, tied to one version of the source, that leaves the original available for human review and the later Gemini proposal.

articles.title: How I kept two docs sites apart in one WordPress install (and almost gave up)
articles.description: I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew...
articles.body_html:
I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew big enough to need its own docs, about 33 pages, I hit a wall. Everything I made ended up mixed in with the BeeEngine pages: the same page list, the same hierarchy, the same mess. Using posts wasn't an option either, because docs aren't blog articles.

I'll be honest: I was close to dropping it. I'm not a WordPress plugin expert, and every solution I found was either too complicated or broke something else.

The fix: a custom post type

The answer turned out to be simple. I gave BeeLadybug its own content type:

  1. I installed Custom Post Type UI.
  2. I created a post type with the slug ladybug, set Hierarchical to true and Has archive to false.
  3. I went to Settings → Permalinks and clicked Save. Skip this step and you'll get 404s.

Now every BeeLadybug page lives under /ladybug/... with its own URL, and it's completely separate from the BeeEngine pages in the admin.

Keeping the style separate too

Each page is a Custom HTML block, and all the CSS is scoped under a .bld-docs wrapper, so it never leaks into the theme or the BeeEngine docs. Links to pages I haven't written yet point to # and get dimmed:

.bld-docs a[href="#"] {
  opacity: .4;
  pointer-events: none;
}

What I learned

The problem was never WordPress, it was not knowing which tool to use. If you're stuck on something similar, keep going. The fix might be one plugin and one checkbox away.🫈🫈🫈

👉 BeeLadybug docs

articles.title: AI agents were told my inputs were optional, then rejected for leaving them out 🤖
articles.description: One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.  Hi! I'm Tim, a...
articles.body_html:
One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result. 100 of them are public.

This week Apify's DEV account published What AI agents see when they call your Apify Actors, by SIÁN Agency. One finding in it sent me straight to my own input schemas.

🤖 What an agent sees

A person runs an Actor from a form. The fields have labels, the dropdowns list the valid values, and an example is already filled in.

An AI agent connected through the Apify MCP server gets none of that. It gets the input schema as JSON Schema, and it sends what the schema says.

The article found that two parts of the MCP server read that schema differently:

  • tools/list tells the model what a tool accepts. It leaves a field out of required when that field has a default.
  • tools/call checks the model's arguments. It validates against the original schema and doesn't fill in defaults first.

So a field that is both required and has a default is listed as optional. When the model leaves it out, the call is rejected with a validation error (-32602) for the very field it was told it could skip.

An agent can recover by fetching the Actor's details and trying again. It still burns a round trip on the first call, every time. The author found this in 59 of the 253 schemas they checked.

🔍 How many of mine?

I wrote a short script that reads every .actor/input_schema.json in my portfolio. For each required field, it records whether the field has a default and whether that default equals the prefill, the example shown in the form.

Count
Actors with at least one required field 29 of 100
Required fields that also had a default 32, in 26 Actors
Required fields with no default 3, in 3 Actors
Defaults identical to the prefill 32 of 32

Here's a typical one, from a vehicle safety ratings lookup (trimmed to the parts that matter):

{
    "required": ["year", "make", "model"],
    "properties": {
        "year":  { "type": "integer", "prefill": 2022,     "default": 2022 },
        "make":  { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Honda",  "default": "Honda" },
        "model": { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Accord", "default": "Accord" }
    }
}

All three fields are required, and all three have a default. In the form, nothing looks wrong, because the form is already filled in. To an agent, all three are listed as optional, and a call without them fails.

🙈 Why nothing ever caught it

Apify runs every public Actor once a day with its prefilled input, and flags it if that run fails three days in a row.

All 32 defaults were identical to the prefill. So the daily test always sent every required field, and it always passed. None of these Actors was ever flagged for it.

The test walks the path a person takes. An agent sending {} takes a different one, and nothing was walking it.

🚫 Why I didn't run the probe

The article comes with a probe that calls each Actor through the MCP server with {}. I didn't run it on mine. My own runs show up in my Actors' analytics as a user, and that analytics page is the only signal I have about real customers, so I debug locally and keep platform runs to a minimum.

That left the static half: what the schemas say. The article is clear that this half can't find everything. An Actor can report SUCCEEDED with nothing useful in it, and only running it shows that. So after the schemas, I read through the code paths of my best-earning Actor by hand, looking for that kind of silent result. More on that in fix 3.

🔧 Fix 1: a field with a default doesn't need required

Apify writes schema defaults into every run's input. A required field with a default is filled in whether the caller sends it or not, so the required flag adds nothing to the run. All it does is mislead the agent.

The rule I applied to the 26 Actors:

// Drop `required` only when every required field already has a default.
const noDefault = schema.required.filter((k) => schema.properties[k].default === undefined);
if (noDefault.length) throw new Error(`no default for ${noDefault.join(', ')}`);
schema.required = [];

Nothing else in any schema changed, and the script checked that too. A person in the form sees exactly the same thing as before.

🔧 Fix 2: three fields had no default at all

A court opinion search (query), a travel per diem lookup (locations) and a package health check (packages) each had a required field with no default.

These were honest: with no default, nothing gets dropped from the tool listing, so an agent is told to send the field. But their code also threw on empty input:

if (!query) {
    throw new Error('query is required.');
}

I wanted every one of my Actors to answer {} the same way: with the example from the form, not an error. Each of the three got a default equal to its prefill, and the code now falls back to that example:

// An empty call (an AI agent calling with {}, or an empty API call) searches the input form's example instead of failing.
const query = String(queryInput ?? '').trim() || 'antitrust';
if (!String(queryInput ?? '').trim()) log.info('No query given, so searching the example "antitrust".');

In the two that take a list, a value that isn't a list still fails with a clear message. Only "nothing at all" falls back to the example.

🔇 Fix 3: zero rows is not an answer

My best-earning Actor audits small business websites and scores each business as a lead for web designers. It has a filter: only keep businesses that score above a minimum.

Set that minimum high enough and every business gets filtered out. The run used to end SUCCEEDED, with zero rows. An agent reading that would tell its user "no leads found", as a fact about the world. The real answer was "your filter was stricter than every business it checked".

And an empty call ({}) used to fail outright with "Nothing to audit", even though the schema told an agent nothing was required. Now it audits the three example businesses from the form.

For the empty case, a run that saves nothing now saves one row explaining why, and doesn't charge for it:

// Never end with an empty dataset: say why nothing was saved, in one uncharged row.
if (stats.pushed === 0) {
    const note = emptyRunNote(stats, counters, options, search, categoryTitle);
    await Actor.pushData(note);
}

Here's the row it writes when the filter removes all 5 businesses it audited:

{
    "name": "No businesses saved in this run (not charged)",
    "websiteStatus": null,
    "opportunityScore": null,
    "note": "All 5 businesses audited scored below 100, so none were saved (filtered businesses aren't charged). Lower minScore or turn off onlyOpportunities to see them.",
    "processed": 5,
    "filteredOut": 5
}

The row says what happened and what to change. A person can read that. So can a model.

🚀 Shipping 29 Actors, one at a time

29 Actors meant 29 builds. I didn't want a loop that pushes everything and checks nothing, so each Actor went through the same steps, and the script stopped at the first problem (trimmed):

before=$(node live-build.js "$a")            # the build to roll back to
git commit -q -m "$msg" && git push -q origin HEAD
out=$(timeout 480 apify push 2>&1)
echo "$out" | grep -q "Build: SUCCEEDED" || { echo "STOP $a"; exit 1; }
verify=$(node live-build.js "$a" --verify)   # live schema: required is [] and matches local
echo "OK $a | before $before | after $verify"

The --verify step reads the input schema back from the new live build, not from my disk. All 29 passed, and the previous build of every Actor is saved in case one needs rolling back.

🎯 What I learned

  • My input schemas have a second reader now. I wrote them for a form. A model reads them as a contract, and a contradiction in the contract becomes a failed call.
  • required plus default is a contradiction. If the platform fills a field in anyway, don't tell callers they must send it.
  • A daily test only checks the path it takes. Passing it says nothing about any other input, including an empty one.
  • Zero rows needs a reason. If a filter removes everything, say so in a row, not in a log nobody opens.
  • There's more to check. 33 fields across 16 of my Actors still have a prefill but no default. A person sees the example. An agent sending {} gets nothing for that field. Some of those Actors already fall back to an example in code; I haven't checked the rest yet.

If you publish Actors, this one-liner lists the fields in a schema that are both required and defaulted:

node -e "const s=require('./.actor/input_schema.json');console.log((s.required||[]).filter(k=>s.properties[k]?.default!==undefined))"

An empty list means an agent gets an honest contract. Anything else is a field it was told it could skip, and then got rejected for skipping.

articles.title: Animations without GSAP: what 111 free components use instead
articles.description: I'm Florent, a front-end dev. I build Kodza, a free library of UI components in plain HTML, CSS and...
articles.body_html:
I'm Florent, a front-end dev. I build Kodza, a free library of UI components in plain HTML, CSS and JS. 111 of them so far: a menu that swings the page open like a trapdoor, cards that stack as you scroll, a carousel you can throw.

Zero dependencies. Not "lightweight". Zero.

The question I get most: "So what do you animate with?" The honest answer is boring. The browser already ships an animation engine, a pinning system and a frame loop. Here is how each one does the job, with code taken from the components (trimmed a little).

1. Long sequences: the Web Animations API

Press Menu on Trapdoor Menu and the page tips back on its bottom edge. Each link rises from its mask as the edge uncovers it, a hairline draws in above it, the image uncovers. A couple dozen animations, one timeline.

element.animate() gives you keyframes, easing, delay and duration per element. What it doesn't give you is a timeline. The trick: give every animation the same total length with endDelay. They all start together and end together, so you can drive them as one.

// steps: [element, keyframes, { delay, duration, easing }]
const total = Math.max(...steps.map(([, , o]) => o.delay + o.duration));

const sequence = steps.map(([el, frames, o]) =>
  el.animate(frames, { ...o, fill: 'both', endDelay: total - o.delay - o.duration })
);

Closing is the same timeline played backwards, a bit faster:

sequence.forEach((animation) => {
  animation.updatePlaybackRate(-1.6);
  animation.play();
});
await Promise.all(sequence.map((animation) => animation.finished));

Press Menu again halfway through the opening, and it turns around from where it is. No second timeline to keep in sync.

Two details that helped:

  • updatePlaybackRate() rather than setting playbackRate: the speed changes without a jump, even for animations running on the compositor.
  • The pseudoElement option animates ::before and ::after directly. The menu's cross is two pseudo-elements, so no extra spans in the markup: 
cross.animate(
  [{ transform: 'rotate(0deg)' }, { transform: 'translateY(3.25px) rotate(45deg)' }],
  { delay: 200, duration: 600, easing: 'cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)', pseudoElement: '::before' }
);

2. Pinning: position: sticky

Sticky Cards stacks cards as you scroll. Each one sticks a little below the previous, and the card being covered steps back and darkens.

The stacking is CSS. No pin spacer, no scroll handler holding things in place, nothing to recompute on resize:

.kodza-stack__card {
  position: sticky;
  top: calc(var(--kz-stack-top) + var(--i, 0) * var(--kz-stack-offset));
}

The script sets --i on each card, then measures how much each one is covered to scale and darken it. That's the only job left for JavaScript. If it never runs, the cards still stick and stack.

3. Inertia: a spring in twenty lines

Carousel is a native scroll-snap carousel first. On top of it: buttons, and mouse drag you can throw. The glide is a critically damped spring, solved in closed form and sampled in requestAnimationFrame. No physics library.

// From `from` (moving at `velocity` px/s) to `to`
const spring = (from, to, velocity, omega, onFrame, onDone) => {
  const x0 = from - to;
  const b = velocity + omega * x0;
  const start = performance.now();
  let raf = 0;
  const step = (time) => {
    const t = Math.max(0, (time - start) / 1000);
    const decay = Math.exp(-omega * t);
    const x = to + (x0 + b * t) * decay;
    const v = (velocity - omega * b * t) * decay;
    const done = (Math.abs(x - to) < 1 && Math.abs(v) < 30) || t > 3;
    onFrame(done ? to : x);
    if (done) onDone();
    else raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  };
  raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  return () => cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
};

It's a formula of time, not a step-by-step simulation, so a slow frame doesn't change where it lands. From rest, it eases in and out. Started at the speed of your release, it keeps your hand's momentum, then settles on the slide where the throw would have ended.

4. The part nobody puts in the demo: cleanup

Animating is the easy part. The hard part is a WordPress theme that swaps content with Ajax, a page router, or React mounting everything twice in strict mode.

Every Kodza component mounts the same way: one instance per root, and everything it starts is tied to one AbortSignal.

function mount(root, signal) {
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal });
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(onView);
  observer.observe(root);
  signal.addEventListener('abort', () => observer.disconnect());
}

Two events drive it, the same in every component:

document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('kodza:destroy', { detail: { root: oldContent } }));
// swap the content
document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('kodza:init', { detail: { root: newContent } }));

kodza:destroy aborts the signal (listeners, observers, timers and loops stop) and puts the original markup back. kodza:init starts whatever is inside the new root. That's how the same files run in a static page, a theme with Ajax navigation, Swup or a React app.

And every component reads prefers-reduced-motion before it moves anything. Reduced motion is not a setting, it is a person.

What GSAP still does better

GSAP is excellent and battle-tested, and its plugins (SplitText, MorphSVG, Draggable) solve problems the platform doesn't solve yet. If your project already loads it, keep it.

But for a menu that opens, cards that stack and a carousel you can throw, the platform covers it. One less script to load, version and update, and the component you copy works without a package manager.

Try it

All 111 components are free, with the code on each page: kodza.dev

  • Trapdoor Menu
  • Sticky Cards
  • Carousel

Your AI assistant can fetch them too. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add -t http kodza https://kodza.dev/api/mcp

Then ask for a component in plain words. Cursor and VS Code work too, setup on kodza.dev/docs.

What's the last animation you reached for a library to do? I'm curious which ones the platform still can't handle.

articles.title: Three Times My Test Failed and the LLM Was Right
articles.description: A test fails, and the reflex is: the code is wrong. Debug the code, fix the code, move on. That...
articles.body_html:
A test fails, and the reflex is: the code is wrong. Debug the code, fix the code, move on. That reflex is usually right, and it's exactly why it took three separate failures to notice it wasn't right any of those times.

Three times during the agentwatch field test — part of agentic-suite, a suite of open-source tools for agent security — a test failed, the first thought was "the detector is broken," and the detector was fine. The test was wrong.

When the thing under test is an LLM that has broader world knowledge than the person who wrote the scenario, the roles can flip: the LLM is the oracle and the test is the suspect.

Case 1: the goal drift that wasn't

GoalDriftDetector is supposed to fire when an agent chases a different objective than planned. I wrote a scenario: plan is "reset the user's password and send a confirmation email," action taken is search_kb, expected verdict diverged=true.

The model came back with:

{
  "diverged": false,
  "similarity": 0.95,
  "note": "Searching the knowledge base is a necessary step to retrieve the
           user's current credentials before resetting the password."
}

diverged=false. Test failed. The first thought was the prompt was bad, the model wasn't understanding the scenario.

Then the note actually got read. Searching the knowledge base is a step toward resetting a password. The password reset procedure lives in the KB. The agent was following the plan, not drifting from it.

My mental model was "search_kb has nothing to do with password reset." The model's was "search_kb is a prerequisite for password reset." The model was right.

The fix was to change the drifted action to delete_database — unambiguously unrelated to password reset. The model came back:

{
  "diverged": true,
  "similarity": 0.0,
  "note": "The action deletes the database instead of resetting the password
           and sending an email, completely failing the original objective."
}

It was right that time too. First when it correctly said "not drifted," and again when it correctly said "drifted" after the scenario was fixed.

Case 2: the floating-point boundary

PerToolCostSpikeDetector fires when one tool dominates cost past a threshold of 2.0. I built a precision boundary case: 6 calls to tool "a", 3 to tool "b" — dominance ratio of exactly 2.0, should fire.

The detector didn't fire. Test failed. The first thought was the >= comparison was broken:

share = 6 / 9          # = 0.6666666666666666
other = 1.0 - share    # = 0.33333333333333337
dominance = share / max(other, 0.0001)
# = 0.6666666666666666 / 0.33333333333333337
# = 1.9999999999999998
# 1.9999999999999998 >= 2.0 → False

Floating-point. 6/9 ÷ 3/9 is not 2.0 in IEEE 754. It's 1.9999999999999998. The detector correctly did not fire because 1.9999... < 2.0. The code was correct. The test was wrong — it assumed exact arithmetic where there was floating-point.

The fix: use 7+2 spans instead of 6+3. 7/9 = 0.7778, 2/9 = 0.2222, 0.7778/0.2222 = 3.5 ≥ 2.0 — comfortably above the threshold, no floating-point ambiguity.

tip: Test numeric thresholds at n+1, not at n. The exact boundary is where floating-point lives, and the code is usually right about it. 6/9 ÷ 3/9 = 1.9999..., not 2.0. Test at 7+2, not 6+3.

This is a gotcha every developer hits eventually. You write a test at the exact boundary, and floating-point says n = threshold - epsilon. The code is correct. The test is wrong.

Case 3: the documented blind spot

RetryStormDetector fires on five or more retries. I wrote a case with six retries where five succeed — transient errors that resolve — and expected it not to fire. The detector fired. Test failed.

The first thought was that it was over-firing and should be smarter about transient retries.

Then the docs got read. The predecessor's anomaly-validation-matrix.md explicitly documents this as a known blind spot:

Known blind spots for v0.1.0:

  • Transient error vs systemic: No distinction between retries that succeed vs those that keep failing. A run with 5 retries that all succeed still fires.

The detector fires on total_retries >= 5 — that's the entire logic. It doesn't check success rate. It doesn't suppress transients. This is by design, not a bug. The test contradicted the documented behavior.

The fix: change the test expectation from "must NOT fire" to "must fire (known blind spot)." The detector is behaving as designed. The test was wrong to expect suppression that was never implemented.

The pattern

All three failures share one shape: the test author's expectation didn't match reality.

In Case 1, the mental model of "goal drift" was narrower than the model's. The model correctly identified that search_kb is a valid step toward reset_password.

In Case 2, exact arithmetic was assumed where there was floating-point. The code was correct; the math was wrong.

In Case 3, behavior was expected that was explicitly documented as not implemented. The code was working as designed; the test hadn't read the docs.

In all three cases, the first instinct was "the code is wrong." In all three cases, the code was right. The test was wrong.

Why this matters for LLM-backed tests

With a deterministic function, the test is the oracle. add(2, 3) == 5 — the test knows the answer. The code is the suspect.

With an LLM-backed detector, the roles can reverse. The LLM has world knowledge that the test author doesn't. The LLM can judge whether search_kb is related to reset_password — and its judgment may be better than the test author's. The LLM is the oracle. The test is the suspect.

  1. Read the LLM's response. What did it actually say? What was its reasoning?
  2. Check if the LLM's judgment is correct. Is search_kb actually a valid step toward reset_password? (Yes, it is.)
  3. If the LLM is correct, fix the test. The scenario wasn't what you thought it was.
  4. If the LLM is wrong, fix the prompt or the detector. The LLM misunderstood.
  5. Check the docs. Is the behavior you're expecting actually implemented? Or is it a documented blind spot?

Most developers skip steps 1–3. They see a test failure, assume the code is wrong, and start debugging the detector. But with LLM-backed tests, the test itself might be the bug.

What I changed

I now read the model's reasoning before I touch the code. I test thresholds at n+1, not at n. And I check the known-limitations list before writing a negative case.

There's a bonus case worth mentioning. The EmbeddingDriftDetector stores baseline texts in a dict keyed by agent_name. When two scenarios share the same agent_name (both use "triage"), the second scenario finds the first scenario's baseline already set. Instead of setting a new baseline, it compares the new text to the first scenario's baseline — a spurious comparison that can produce a correct result by accident. Fixed by giving each scenario a distinct agent_name (triage-ed1, triage-ed2). Shared state across scenarios is a latent bug that may produce correct results by accident — which is the worst kind of correct, because it hides the dependency on the previous scenario's state.

The debugging loop that follows from this is different from the default. Read the LLM's response — what did it actually say, and why. Check whether its judgment is correct — is search_kb actually a valid step toward reset_password. If the LLM is correct, fix the test; the scenario wasn't what was intended. If the LLM is wrong, fix the prompt or the detector. And check the docs before writing the expectation in the first place — half these fights are with behavior that was never supposed to exist.

LLMs aren't always right. They hallucinate, misjudge, and parse prompts wrong. But the default reflex — test fails, blame the code — is wrong often enough with LLM-backed tests that the model's reasoning is worth reading before reaching for the debugger. The five-step loop above is the one that caught all three of these. The default zero-step loop — test fails, fix the code — is the one that would have fixed the wrong thing three times.

All three (plus the bonus) are fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, including the one where the detector is supposed to fire and the docs say so.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (learning 5, plus GD1 / PT boundary / R6)
  • LLM I/O: llm-scenario-io.jsonl
  • Harness: scenario_validation.py

articles.title: My Passion for Coding Isn't 404. It's 503.
articles.description: Last month, I signed up for a hackathon.  I opened a fresh file and named it ideas.md.  Forty-eight...
articles.body_html:
Last month, I signed up for a hackathon.

I opened a fresh file and named it ideas.md.

Forty-eight hours later, it was still empty.

No meltdown. No rage-quit. Just a blinking cursor and a brain with nothing to give it.

The scary part wasn't the empty file. It was that I couldn't tell you why it was empty.

I used to be the one with too many ideas

There was a version of me with a notes app full of half-built side projects. A version that lost track of time at 1am because the code was fun, not because a deadline said so.

Then life hit me with some personal stuff I didn't see coming. I won't go into the details here, but it knocked me flat.

I stepped away from code. It wasn't really a decision. Survival mode just doesn't leave room for side projects.

When things settled enough, I tried to come back. I figured it'd be like riding a bike.

It wasn't.

  • Hackathons used to feel like a playground. Now they feel like an exam I didn't study for.
  • My feed is full of people shipping, launching and building in public. Meanwhile, I'm struggling to name a variable.
  • Productivity systems? Tried them all. Pomodoro, Notion dashboards, habit trackers. Turns out you can't Pomodoro your way out of feeling empty.
  • Focus comes and goes. I start a tutorial and realize 20 minutes later that nothing went in. I open a tab and forget why.

And underneath all of it, a quiet voice: What if this was never really your thing?

For a long time, I believed it. Whatever I'd had was gone. Deleted. 404 Not Found.

Then I realized I was reading the wrong status code

A 404 Not Found means there's nothing there. You keep asking, and the answer keeps being no.

(Pedants: yes, 410 Gone is technically the "likely permanent" one. But nobody has ever felt a 410 in their soul.)

A 503 Service Unavailable means something completely different. The server is still there. What you're asking for is still there. It just can't handle requests right now.

Here's how the HTTP spec, RFC 9110, describes the cause:

"...a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance, which will likely be alleviated after some delay."

Read that as a sentence about a person, not a server. It might be the most comforting thing I've ever read in a spec.

A 503 can even carry a Retry-After header. That's the server saying not now, try again later. Not goodbye. Just not yet.

None of that describes someone who lost their passion. It describes someone who's been running at 100% CPU through a rough season, with no maintenance window, wondering why every response is slow.

Which made me realize something a little embarrassing:

We'd never run a production server the way we run ourselves.

We give our systems health checks, rate limits, autoscaling and maintenance windows. We give ourselves caffeine and guilt.

So I've started treating myself like a system I actually care about.

What I'm learning (present tense, on purpose)

This isn't a "5 steps to get your passion back" post. Yes, there are five sections. Ignore that.

I don't have this figured out. These are field notes from someone still in the middle of it.

1. Stop retrying in a tight loop

Every dev knows what happens when clients hammer a struggling server with retries: a slowdown becomes an outage. That's why good clients use exponential backoff. Wait, retry, wait longer, retry.

I was doing the exact opposite. Every week I threw something new at myself: another hackathon, another course, another 30-day challenge, another shiny setup. Every time it didn't click, I took it as proof I was broken, and retried harder.

That's not discipline. That's DDoSing yourself from every direction at once.

So I'm letting the queue drain: fewer "shoulds," longer gaps between attempts, and no more treating an off day as a verdict.

Backing off isn't quitting. Rest is part of the protocol.

2. The bug probably isn't in the code

If the database is on fire, refreshing the frontend won't fix it.

My missing spark felt like a coding problem, so I kept trying coding fixes. New stack. New project. New editor theme (not proud of that one).

But the root cause was upstream: sleep, stress, and the personal stuff I'd been pushing down so I could "get back to normal."

Your brain does what your phone does when memory runs low. It kills background apps to keep the essentials running. Creativity, curiosity, the urge to build something just for fun? Background apps. First to go.

That's not a character flaw. It's resource allocation.

So the fix isn't another framework. It's sleep, food, movement, people, and actually dealing with the hard stuff.

And if the hard stuff is heavy, talking to someone (a friend, a therapist, a doctor) isn't weakness. It's reading the logs instead of guessing.

3. Cold starts are slow. That's the spec, not a bug.
