        SECURITY: identity propagation · least-privilege tools · injection isolation · tenant isolation · secrets in vaults

Design checklist 

CONTROL FLOW     [ ] Deterministic skeleton; agents only where the path is genuinely open-ended        [ ] Every loop (steps, retries, replans, refinements, handoffs, depth) has a code-enforced bound
STATE            [ ] Typed, versioned, event-sourced state; large data by reference                      [ ] Single writer per run; idempotent, order-safe events; pinned model/prompt/tool versions
DURABILITY       [ ] Model and tool calls are recorded steps (activities); orchestrator code deterministic [ ] Write-ahead intent + idempotency keys; in-doubt reconciliation; resume tested at every crash point
TOOLS            [ ] Few, focused, well-described tools per agent; retrieval/routing for large toolsets    [ ] Typed schemas, validated in code; helpful error contract; two-phase for consequential actions
APPROVALS        [ ] Risk-tiered policy in code; proposal-bound, authorized, expiring, fail-closed         [ ] Re-validation on resume; edit-and-approve; audit; fatigue monitoring
MULTI-AGENT      [ ] Typed contracts; minimal shared context; one owner per responsibility                 [ ] Supervisor logic is code; workers least-privileged; handoff topology and loop guards
COMMUNICATION    [ ] Envelope with correlation, schema version, expiry, trace context; validated on receipt [ ] Agent identities and authorization; untrusted-content handling; bounded chatter
RECOVERY         [ ] Failure taxonomy; retries only for idempotent transient errors; circuit breakers       [ ] Repair loops (bounded); compensation for atomic tasks; escalation and dead-letter paths
BUDGETS          [ ] Hierarchical budgets (run → worker → tool); soft wrap-up warnings, hard stops          [ ] Graceful partial results; limits derived from evaluation percentiles; per-tenant caps
MEMORY           [ ] Scoped; write policy; provenance; consolidation and expiry; untrusted when recalled    [ ] User control and erasure
TESTING          [ ] Scripted-model tests; fault injection and crash/resume; replay tests                  [ ] Evaluation on a simulated environment with repeated runs; adversarial/security suite
OPERATIONS       [ ] Traces/metrics/event-log audit; operator console; kill switch; runbooks               [ ] Cost attribution and anomaly alerts

21. Common Pitfalls

Pitfall Why it hurts Better approach
Treating the transcript as the agent's state Lossy, unbounded, unversioned; can't resume or audit Typed, versioned, event-sourced state; derive prompts from it (Section 5)
Calling the model inside durable orchestrator code Nondeterminism breaks replay; duplicates or diverges Wrap every model call in an activity so its result is recorded (Section 8)
Using DateTime.UtcNow, Guid.NewGuid(), or Task.Delay in orchestrators Replay takes a different path Use the orchestration context's time, GUID, and timer APIs (Section 8)
Non-idempotent tools behind retries or resume Duplicate charges, emails, records Idempotency keys, write-ahead intent, in-doubt reconciliation (Section 9)
Changing orchestrator logic with runs in flight In-flight instances fail replay Version orchestrations, additive changes, pin versions, drain old runs (Sections 8-9)
Unbounded orchestration history Slow replay, storage growth ContinueAsNew, small payloads, references to blobs (Section 8)
Letting an approval timeout mean "proceed" Unapproved consequential actions Fail closed; expire pending approvals as not approved (Section 10)
Acting on an old approval without re-checking World changed since approval Re-validate preconditions and the proposal hash on resume (Section 10)
Approval screens that don't show the real action Rubber-stamping; unauthorized effects Show exact arguments/preview and evidence; bind approval to a hash (Section 10)
Giving all tools to every agent Wrong-tool errors, token waste, large blast radius Per-role toolsets, routing, tool retrieval, permission-aware lists (Section 3)
Free-form query/command/data tool parameters Escape hatch for injection and error Typed, narrow parameters turned into parameterized operations (Section 4)
Trusting tool arguments because a schema exists Models still produce invalid/hostile values Validate in code; return helpful errors (Section 4)
Single-step "dangerous" tools A hijacked or confused call executes immediately Two-phase prepare/commit with bound, single-use tokens (Section 4)
Supervisor that is just an LLM in a loop Top-level failures: loops, no validation, no recovery Decomposition by model; validation, ordering, budgets, retries, verification in code (Section 12)
Forwarding full transcripts between agents Context bloat, telephone-game errors Typed task/result contracts with summaries and references (Sections 11-12)
Unbounded handoffs Ping-pong loops, privilege games Explicit topology, handoff caps, loop detection, escalate to a human (Section 13)
Agents trusting each other's messages Injection hops between agents Schema-validate every message; treat as untrusted data (Sections 11, 14)
Retrying everything Duplicate effects; storms against failing tools Classify failures; retry only idempotent transient errors with backoff and circuit breakers (Section 15)
No repair strategy for invalid structured output Brittle runs or infinite re-asking Bounded repair loops with validation feedback, then escalate (Section 15)
Irreversible steps first, approvals after Can't undo; no gate Reversible-by-design actions; irreversible steps last, behind approvals; sagas for atomic tasks (Section 15)
Only a step cap as loop protection Slow, expensive stops; misses low-progress drift Repetition, cycle, and progress detection with an intervention ladder (Section 16)
No give-up tool or success criteria The agent keeps trying An explicit give_up/ask_user; objective acceptance criteria for refinement loops (Section 16)
Budgets as exceptions that corrupt state Partial work lost; crashes at the limit Soft warnings, graceful partial results, reserved wrap-up allowance (Section 17)
Sub-agent budgets that can exceed the parent's Total cost unbounded Hierarchical budgets where child usage charges the parent (Section 17)
Choosing autonomy because it demos well Unpredictable cost, behavior, and risk in production Start deterministic; promote steps to agentic only with evidence; keep determinism around side effects (Section 18)
Evaluating only happy paths Loops, crashes, and edge cases ship Scripted-model tests, crash/resume fault injection, replay tests, adversarial suites (Section 19)
No operator controls Can't stop or inspect a misbehaving run Console to inspect, fork, cancel, and disable tools/agents; alerts and runbooks (Section 19)

Quick Reference Table

Topic Core idea Practical takeaway
ReAct Thought → Action → Observation loop Native tool calling by default; step records; don't trust visible reasoning as evidence
Planning loops Plan as validated data, execute, monitor, replan Validate DAG and tools; parallelize independent steps; verify by real state; bound replans
Tool selection Selection degrades as toolboxes grow Curate per role, route, retrieve tools, permission-aware lists, disambiguating descriptions
Tool schema design Schema = contract for a probabilistic caller Few typed params, enums, validation in code, helpful errors, two-phase tools, idempotency keys
State management Typed, versioned, event-sourced state Messages are derived; single writer; large data by reference; versioned schemas
Memory Short-term compaction; long-term scoped, policy-gated Write policy, provenance, consolidation, expiry; recalled memory is untrusted data
Workflow orchestration Control flow as an explicit graph Deterministic skeleton, bounded agent steps, checkpoint after each node
Durable execution Persisted progress, replayable orchestrators Model/tool calls as activities; deterministic orchestrator; ContinueAsNew; version in-flight runs
Checkpointing Write-ahead intent + idempotency Reconcile in-doubt calls; at-least-once + idempotent = exactly-once effect; pin versions
Human approvals Durable, authorized, expiring, bound to the proposal Risk-tiered policy; fail closed; re-validate on resume; edit-and-approve
Multi-agent collaboration Specialization at the cost of complexity Typed contracts; one owner per task; least privilege; measure against a single-agent baseline
Supervisor-worker Coordinator decomposes, workers execute Supervisor logic in code; validated results; per-worker budgets; partial results first-class
Handoffs Control transfers to another agent Explicit topology; compact briefing; privileges don't transfer; loop guards; escalate to humans
Communication protocols MCP (agent↔tools), A2A (agent↔agent), typed envelopes Schema-validate, authenticate agents, bound chatter, treat messages as untrusted
Failure recovery Classify, then remediate Retry idempotent transient errors; repair loops; sagas; escalate; dead-letter; kill switch
Loop prevention Many loop shapes Hard caps + repetition/cycle/progress detection + intervention ladder + give-up exit
Budgets and limits A guaranteed worst case Hierarchical budgets, soft wrap-up, graceful partials, limits from evaluation percentiles
Workflows vs. agents A spectrum Start deterministic; agent proposes, workflow disposes; promote/demote autonomy by evidence
Testing and observing Scripted models, fault injection, replay Crash at every step; exactly-once effects; traces, event-log audit, operator console

Conclusion

The jump from a working agent to a dependable one is almost entirely an exercise in separating concerns: let the model decide what to try, and let code own everything that must be reliable. The ReAct loop gives the model its reasoning-and-acting rhythm; plan-and-execute adds a validated plan as data; tool retrieval and tight, typed, two-phase tool schemas keep its choices accurate and its blast radius small. State lives outside the transcript — typed, versioned, event-sourced — so a run can be audited, forked, and resumed. Workflows make control flow explicit; durable execution (Durable Functions, Temporal, or an event-sourced worker you write yourself) turns every model call and tool call into a recorded step, with write-ahead intent and idempotency keys making crashes, retries, and deployments harmless. Human approvals become durable, authorized, expiring workflow steps bound to the exact proposal, re-validated when the run resumes.

Multi-agent designs earn their complexity only when measurement says a single agent falls short, and then only with typed contracts, one owner per responsibility, least-privilege workers, a supervisor whose logic is code, handoffs with explicit topology and loop guards, and protocols (typed envelopes internally, MCP for tools, A2A across systems) that authenticate agents and treat every message as untrusted. Failures are classified rather than blindly retried; invalid outputs get bounded repair; side effects get compensation; loops are detected by repetition, cycle, and progress signals with an intervention ladder and an explicit way to give up; and hierarchical budgets guarantee a worst case, ending in graceful partial results instead of crashes. Above it all sits the most useful design question: can you write down the steps? If yes, build a deterministic workflow and put the model inside it. If only part is open-ended, put a bounded agent in just that step. Reserve autonomy for genuinely exploratory work — and even there, keep determinism around the actions that matter, test with scripted models and crash-and-resume fault injection, and give operators the tools to see, steer, and stop what the agent is doing. Do that, and agents stop being impressive demos that fail unpredictably and become systems you can run, bound, audit, and trust.

Found this useful? Feel free to star the repo, open an issue with corrections, or share the "the deployment restarted mid-refund and the idempotency key was the only thing between us and a double payment" story that made the case for write-ahead intent and replay-safe design click better than any workflow diagram.

articles.title: LazyDesk AI: Let Your Local AI Handle the Digital Mess 🦥💜
articles.description: LazyDesk AI: Let Your Local AI Handle the Digital Mess 🦥💜   This is a submission for the...
articles.body_html:
LazyDesk AI: Let Your Local AI Handle the Digital Mess 🦥💜

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I Built

Have you ever downloaded a PDF, saved a screenshot, renamed a document three times, and then completely forgotten where you put it?

Same problem, too many files, and somehow the job of organizing them always gets postponed.

That's why I built LazyDesk AI — a local-first, AI-powered file organizer designed to make digital clutter less overwhelming.

Instead of relying entirely on manually organizing files, LazyDesk AI explores how a local language model can help suggest clearer filenames and useful categories based on file metadata.

The goal is simple: spend less time deciding where files belong and more time doing the work that actually matters.

✨ What LazyDesk AI brings to the table:

  • 🗂️ A focused workspace: A dashboard with Overview, File Organizer, Activity, and Settings pages.
  • 🧠 AI-powered suggestions: Gemma 3 running through Ollama can analyze file metadata and generate structured suggestions.
  • 🔌 Local AI status: Check whether the backend can connect to Ollama and whether the model is available.
  • 🎨 A clean interface: A dark, violet-accented UI designed to make organizing feel less like another chore.
  • 🔐 A local-first approach: AI inference runs through Ollama on your own machine rather than requiring a hosted AI API.

The project is still evolving. The dashboard currently includes sample workspace data, and I am working toward a complete folder-selection and organization workflow. I want to be transparent about that: this is a working prototype, not yet a fully automated file manager.

Demo

GitHub repository: Shikha18Shukla/LazyDesk-AI

The repository contains the source code and setup instructions to run the project locally.

The application currently runs locally, so I don't have a public hosted demo to share yet. The next milestone is to connect the folder-selection flow end to end and demonstrate the complete experience with real files.

Code

Explore the project here:

🔗 View LazyDesk AI on GitHub

The project is organized into two main parts:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI, with an endpoint for analyzing file metadata.

The backend communicates with Ollama locally and uses gemma3:4b to request structured AI suggestions.

The repository also includes a README with installation instructions, the API overview, troubleshooting guidance, and the project's roadmap.

How I Built It

The central idea was to build around an open-weight model rather than making a hosted AI service a mandatory dependency.

Here's the architecture:

       User
        |
        v
+----------------------+
| React + TypeScript   |
| LazyDesk AI UI       |
+----------------------+
        |
        v
+----------------------+
| Python + FastAPI     |
| Local API            |
+----------------------+
        |
        v
+----------------------+
| Ollama               |
| Local inference      |
+----------------------+
        |
        v
+----------------------+
| Gemma 3 (4B)         |
| File metadata        |
| analysis and ideas   |
+----------------------+
        |
        v
+----------------------+
| Structured AI        |
| suggestions          |
+----------------------+

1. The interface

I built the frontend using React and TypeScript, with Vite for development. The interface is organized into separate pages so that the project can grow beyond a single file-upload screen.

2. The backend

FastAPI provides the API layer. The health endpoint checks whether Ollama is reachable and whether the configured model is available. The analysis endpoint accepts a filename, extension, and file size, then sends a prompt to the local model.

3. The open-weight model

I chose Gemma 3 (4B) and run it through Ollama.

The model receives file metadata rather than needing the entire file's contents for the current analysis workflow. It is asked to return a structured suggestion that the application can use.

4. Working within real hardware limits

I developed this on a laptop without a dedicated GPU. That made local inference speed an important practical consideration.

It also made the project more interesting: I wanted to explore how useful local AI could be on everyday hardware, rather than assuming everyone has access to an expensive GPU or a paid cloud API.

The current version is a foundation. Connecting real folder selection, adding safe rename and move operations, and measuring performance are still part of the work ahead.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project, open innovation isn't just a way to avoid a paid API. It changes the way the application can be built.

1. More control over personal data

File names can reveal a surprising amount about someone's life: academic work, job applications, personal documents, and projects.

With local inference, the model can process the metadata on the user's own machine. The intended workflow does not require sending that metadata to a third-party AI API. Of course, the actual privacy guarantees still depend on how the application is configured and implemented.

2. No mandatory per-request AI bill

Once the model is downloaded, local inference doesn't require paying a hosted AI provider for every request. Electricity, hardware resources, storage, and setup still have costs, but experimentation becomes much more accessible.

3. Freedom to experiment

Using an open-weight model makes it possible to explore different prompts, change the model, and test different approaches without rebuilding the application around a single closed provider.

4. AI that's closer to the user

A local-first design can reduce dependence on internet connectivity for inference after the model has been downloaded and the local services are running.

For a utility that deals with personal files, that is a meaningful design choice.

Open innovation made it possible for me to experiment with a practical AI-powered desktop utility while learning how the UI, API, and local model work together.

My Agent Session

I used AI-assisted development while building the interface and project structure.

I haven't included a DevRelay session link because I don't have a verified public session URL to share yet. I'd rather leave that out than publish a link that doesn't work.

The Lazy Payoff 🦥

The payoff I'm aiming for is fewer repetitive decisions.

Imagine a folder containing files like:

notes_final.pdf
notes_final_v2.pdf
IMG_20261021_104533.png
download (7).pdf

A future end-to-end version of LazyDesk AI could inspect the metadata, suggest clearer names, and group related files for the user to review.

For example, it might suggest a more descriptive filename for a lecture PDF or recommend grouping screenshots separately from documents.

Those are illustrative examples of the intended workflow, not claims of measured results from the current prototype.

I haven't measured time saved yet. My next step is to test the workflow with a real folder, compare the manual process with AI-assisted suggestions, and record how long each takes.

Because saving time should be demonstrated, not just promised.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma — using Google's Gemma 3 open-weight model through Ollama for local AI-powered file metadata analysis.

I'm entering only the category that directly matches the technology used in this project.

Final Thoughts 💜

LazyDesk AI started with a small idea: what if organizing digital clutter didn't always require another round of manual effort?

Building it has given me an opportunity to explore local inference, open-weight models, API integration, and the practical challenges of making AI useful on everyday hardware.

It isn't finished yet, and that's part of the journey. The next challenge is turning the prototype into a reliable workflow that works with real folders and gives users control over every change.

Because sometimes productivity doesn't mean doing more.

Sometimes it means letting the computer handle a little more of the boring stuff.

Build thoughtfully. Automate carefully. Stay a little lazy. 🦥

Hacktoberfest #HF26Challenge #OpenSourceAI #Gemma #Ollama #Python #React #LocalAI #Productivity

articles.title: Deep dive into the C++ Passkey idiom
articles.description: 1. Motivation: The Problem with friend   In C++, friend is a double-edged sword. If you...
articles.body_html:
1. Motivation: The Problem with friend

In C++, friend is a double-edged sword. If you allow your friend to touch you inappropriately, that would be hurt. If class A befriends another class B, then everything in A becomes visible to B. friend grants all-or-nothing access — which is rarely what you actually want. You usually want your friend to only able to touch a portion of you.

Consider the following scenario. You have a Widget class that must be created through a factory, because the constructor needs to perform some privileged setup (registering with a resource manager, validating invariants, logging, and so on). But the constructor itself has to be public for std::make_unique or for the factory to reach it. The moment it is public, anyone can construct a Widget — and that is a correctness bug waiting to happen.

You might reach for friend:


class WidgetFactory;

class Widget {
    friend class WidgetFactory;   // grants access to EVERYTHING
public:
    Widget(int x) : x_{x} {}
private:
    int x_{};
};

class WidgetFactory {
public:
    static std::unique_ptr<Widget> create(int x) {
        return std::make_unique<Widget>(x);
    }
};

int main()
{
    auto w = WidgetFactory::create(42);   // ok
    // auto bad = std::make_unique<Widget>(42); // also ok! constructor is public, but you dont want this...
}

This "works," but it is a blunt instrument. WidgetFactory now has access to every private member of Widget, not just the constructor. As Widget grows, so does the accidental attack surface. And if you later need to grant the same narrow access to a Debugger class, you add another friend, and the surface widens again.

The question this idiom answers is:

How can I let a specific class touch only a specific portion of my class — and nothing else?

And then now let me introduce the PassKey Idiom.

2. The Classic Solution: A Nested PassKey

The core idea is to make a public function that requires an argument nobody else can construct. That argument is the passkey.

class Widget {
public:
    class PassKey {
        friend class Widget;
        PassKey() = default; // this constructor is private
    };

    Widget(PassKey, int x)
        : x_{x}
    {}

    static std::unique_ptr<Widget> create(int x)
    {
        return std::make_unique<Widget>(PassKey{}, x);
    }

private:
    int x_{};
};

int main()
{
    // auto w1 = Widget{Widget::PassKey{}, 42}; // compile error! cannot access private constructor
    auto w2 = Widget::create(42); // ok
}

A few things are worth calling out:

  • The constructor PassKey() = default; is implicitly private (it is a member of a class whose default access is private), and Widget is its only friend.
  • Widget's constructor is public, so it satisfies the syntactic requirements of std::make_unique. But it is only callable by code that can produce a PassKey — which, in practice, means only Widget itself (or whatever Widget chooses to befriend).
  • In main, the direct construction fails to compile because Widget::PassKey is private. The only way in is through create.

This is a clean, zero-boilerplate solution for a single class. But it does not scale. If you have Widget, Gadget, and Sprocket, you must replicate this nested-class boilerplate in every one of them. Worse, the authorized "friend" is baked into the nested definition, so if you want Widget's constructor callable by both a Factory and a Debugger, you either befriend both inside PassKey or duplicate the pattern. How to solve this? we can use a template!

3. Scaling Up: The Templated PassKey

The templated PassKey decouples the mechanism from the class it protects. You define it once, and any class can use it:

template <typename T>
class Passkey {
    friend T;             // only T can construct a Passkey<T>
    Passkey() = default;  // private: no one else can create one
};

Now the authorized class can create a passkey, and unauthorized code cannot:

class WidgetFactory;
class WidgetDebugger;

class Widget {
public:
    // Public constructor, but only callable by whoever can make a Passkey<WidgetFactory>
    Widget(Passkey<WidgetFactory>, int x)
        : x_{x}
    {}

    // A separate, narrower door for the debugger
    void dump(Passkey<WidgetDebugger>) const { /* ... */ }

private:
    int x_{};
};

class WidgetFactory {
public:
    static std::unique_ptr<Widget> create(int x) {
        return std::make_unique<Widget>(Passkey<WidgetFactory>{}, x);
    }
};

class WidgetDebugger {
public:
    void inspect(const Widget& w) {
        w.dump(Passkey<WidgetDebugger>{});
    }
};

int main()
{
    auto w = WidgetFactory::create(42);   // ok
    WidgetDebugger{}.inspect(*w);          // ok

    // auto bad = std::make_unique<Widget>(Passkey<WidgetFactory>{}, 1); // error
    // WidgetDebugger{}.inspect(...) can't call Widget's ctor; Factory can't call dump()
}

The design now has two key properties:

  1. Per-function granularity. Widget's constructor admits only WidgetFactory. Widget::dump admits only WidgetDebugger. Neither can use the other's door. No friend grants blanket access.
  2. Reusable mechanism. Passkey<T> is written once and works for any number of classes. There is no nested-class boilerplate to copy.

A subtle but important point: std::make_unique cannot construct the Passkey for you. The authorized class must explicitly pass Passkey<WidgetFactory>{} into the constructor call. That is by design — make_unique is not the privileged party; the caller is.

Improvement you can made if you are using C++20

C++20 does not fundamentally change the PassKey mechanism. There is no concept that replaces it, because concepts constrain types, whereas PassKey constrains who can produce a token. The two compose nicely, though: if you are building a generic system where the set of authorized callers is itself parameterized, you can write

#include <type_traits>

// Marker: only types deriving from this may be a Caller.
struct Privileged {};

// Passkey<T> only exists if T is privileged.
template <typename T>
    requires std::is_base_of_v<Privileged, T>
class Passkey {
    friend T;
    Passkey() = default;
};

class Widget {
public:
    Widget(Passkey<class Factory>, int x) : x_{x} {}
private:
    int x_{};
};

// Factory opts in — so it can make a Passkey<Factory>.
class Factory : Privileged {
public:
    static Widget create(int x) { return Widget(Passkey<Factory>{}, x); }
};

// Sneaky does NOT opt in — so Passkey<Sneaky> won't compile.
class Sneaky {
public:
    // Widget w{Passkey<Sneaky>{}, 1};  // error: constraint not satisfied
};

That's the whole idea. Widget's constructor is public, but the only way to call it is to hand it a Passkey<Factory> — and only Factory can construct one, because Factory is the friend. The requires clause adds one extra guarantee: you can't even write Passkey<X> unless X derives from Privileged, so unauthorized types fail at the template level instead of at the friend level.

4. Group Permissions: Variadic Friends (C++26)

The templated PassKey has one remaining friction point. Suppose a single function should be callable by several authorized classes — say a Factory, a Debugger, and a Serializer. Before C++26, you cannot write friend Ts...; expanding a parameter pack in a friend declaration is ill-formed. The workarounds are ugly: manual overloads, a combined passkey type, or a chain of nested friends.

C++26 fixes this with variadic friends (P2893R3). You can now expand a pack directly:

#include <iostream>

// C++26: variadic friends — one passkey authorizes a whole pack of types.
template <typename... Ts>
class Passkey {
    friend Ts...;
    Passkey() = default;
};

class Factory;
class Debugger;
class Serializer;

class Widget {
public:
    // Only Factory, Debugger, and Serializer can call this.
    void secretInit(Passkey<Factory, Debugger, Serializer>) {
        std::cout << "Widget initialized\n";
    }
};

// Each authorized type can build the passkey — and thus call secretInit.
class Factory {
public:
    void make(Widget& w) { w.secretInit(Passkey<Factory, Debugger, Serializer>{}); }
};

class Debugger {
public:
    void poke(Widget& w) { w.secretInit(Passkey<Factory, Debugger, Serializer>{}); }
};

class Serializer {
public:
    void save(Widget& w) { w.secretInit(Passkey<Factory, Debugger, Serializer>{}); }
};

// Not in the pack — cannot construct the passkey.
class Intruder {
public:
    // void tryIt(Widget& w) { w.secretInit(Passkey<Factory, Debugger, Serializer>{}); }
    //   ^ error: Passkey ctor is private; Intruder is not a friend.
};

int main()
{
    Widget w;
    Factory{}.make(w);        // ok
    Debugger{}.poke(w);       // ok
    Serializer{}.save(w);     // ok
}

This makes the "group permission" case a one-liner and removes the need for the combined-type hack. It is a small language feature, but for the PassKey idiom it is a meaningful ergonomic win: the passkey now expresses "these N types, and no others" directly in the type system.

5. Performance and Trade-offs

Runtime cost

In theory, passing an empty object by value could cost a register or a stack slot. In practice, in optimized builds, it is a zero-cost abstraction. Because Passkey has no data members and the parameter is unnamed, the optimizer elides it entirely at -O1 and above. There is no runtime check, no branch, no token comparison — the entire mechanism lives in the type system and disappears in the emitted code.

The one caveat

If the protected function is not inlined (defined in a separate translation unit, and LTO is disabled), the calling convention may still require passing a byte for the empty class to satisfy the ABI. This is a minor, usually irrelevant cost. For header-only or inlined usage — which is the common case — there is no overhead at all.

Compile-time cost

Slightly more template instantiation (one specialization per authorized type), and slightly longer function signatures. This is the real price, but it is usually trivial.

Readability trade-offs

  • Signatures get noisier: Widget(Passkey<Factory>, int) is visually heavier than Widget(int).
  • The unnamed parameter convention (see below) is what keeps it readable; without it, reviewers wonder what the argument is for.
  • The mechanism is compile-time enforced, so the compiler error when someone tries to bypass it is clear — but the reason the parameter exists is not obvious to a reader seeing the class for the first time. A brief comment on the constructor is worth the cost.

6. Idiomatic Usage and Best Practices

  • Leave the parameter unnamed. Write void foo(Passkey<T>), not void foo(Passkey<T> key). The unnamed parameter signals "this is a token, not data — it carries no information and is never used in the body."
  • Mark the constructor explicit if you are being defensive. explicit Passkey() = default; is not strictly required — the private access already blocks unauthorized construction — but it guards against brace-initialization surprises and makes intent explicit. It is harmless and recommended for older-standard compatibility (C++17 or earlier).
  • Prefer the templated form. The nested form is fine as a teaching example, but the templated form is the one to use in production.
  • Document the contract. A one-line comment — // only Factory may construct Widget — saves future readers from reverse-engineering the idiom.

8. Summary

  • friend is all-or-nothing; the PassKey idiom gives you per-function, per-caller access control.
  • The nested PassKey is the minimal teaching form; the templated Passkey<T> is the idiomatic production form.
  • C++26 variadic friends (friend Ts...) turns "group permissions" into a one-liner, removing the last piece of friction.
  • It is a zero-cost abstraction in optimized builds; the cost is compile-time and readability, not runtime.
  • Use it for restricted constructors and sensitive methods; use Attorney-Client when you need to expose members instead.

Happy coding!

articles.title: I Tested img2interior with Codex: A Room and a 95 MB Runtime
articles.description: AI-assisted disclosure: Codex assisted with research, code and writing. Measurements, failure cases...
articles.body_html:
AI-assisted disclosure: Codex assisted with research, code and writing. Measurements, failure cases and limitations are retained from the original article.

Originally published by Alicia on 2026-10-22: Digital Garden by Alicia.

img2interior worked in this iterative Codex test, with local Windows fixes and a viewer lifecycle repair. It produced an editable Blender scene, a runtime GLB with a Three.js viewer, and a separate portable GLB. The room is a simplified interpretation of one synthetic reference, with no measured reconstruction claim.

The largest practical finding was the payload. The runtime GLB was 2.67 MB, but its required lightmaps and reflection probe brought the declared total to 95.10 MB. The standalone portable file was 8.80 MB. The full desktop workflow passed after review and repair; no physical phone was tested.

This is an actual render from a fresh process opening the final master. The geometric artwork, uniform stone, simplified upholstery and schematic trees show where the reconstruction stops.

Inspect the static portable model, download the editable study, or read the machine-readable desktop results. The online preview is a separate static consumer; it does not reproduce the full PBR viewer's cloth simulation.

One synthetic reference, a new scene builder

The user selected the project's public synthetic living-room reference: 2752×1536 pixels, with full-height glazing, an ivory sofa, a pale round table, a dark chair and a walnut cabinet. It was not a greenhouse photograph. The reference remains linked at its source and is not redistributed in the download.

img2interior is an agent workflow for authoring a Blender scene, rather than a pretrained image-to-mesh model. In the current Codex desktop conversation, I wrote a scene-specific Python builder using the package's reusable geometry helpers. I did not call its bundled Oak/Linen room recipe or run Claude Code.

The room has actual shell and furniture geometry, glazing, curtains, UV-mapped surfaces and authored lighting: 131 meshes, 46,544 triangles and 12 semantic components. I estimated dimensions in metres, using a roughly 3.1-metre sofa as an anchor. Hidden construction and the camera remain authored assumptions. Native authoring uses Z-up; the glTF exports use Y-up.

This was not a fresh-session, unchanged-prompt benchmark. I preserved failed renders, changed the builder and checked the results. The earlier Codex machine-skill test follows the same distinction between using a skill and accepting its first output.

Setup and the Windows interventions

The test used img2interior 0.3.1, img2 CLI 0.4.0, Python 3.11.14, bpy 4.3.0 and NumPy 1.26.4. The workstation ran Windows 11, a Ryzen 9 9950X and an RTX 5070 Ti. The observed browser was Chromium 155 through ANGLE D3D11. Codex ran in the current desktop conversation; the CLI version readback was 0.144.1.

I registered the package in an isolated harness home and host fixture. Doctor returned zero failures and zero warnings; sync returned zero drift. That verifies the isolated fixture. It does not establish that a newly restarted user Codex host discovered the installed skill.

Three Windows issues needed attention:

  • An inherited OCIO setting pointed Blender at an incompatible studio configuration. Clearing OCIO only in the authoring child process fixed preflight while preserving the workstation setting.
  • The exporter wrote a backslash in the source-image URL. The viewer rejected it. A local Path.as_posix() change fixed that field, with the original retained for rollback.
  • Python 3.12 reported different path-stat and file-stat ctime values, triggering the file-change audit. Running the unchanged checks with Python 3.11 passed. The delivery contract also needed an equivalent relative root because its drive path was classified as a URL.

The downloadable study contains the builder, inputs, generated linen maps, packed master, portable model, applicable notices and the viewer lifecycle patch. Install the pinned official toolkit separately to rebuild. The archive excludes the reference image, environments, production garden plants and the large runtime sidecars.

Render, reject, repair, then bake

The first native render took 5.44 seconds. I rejected it: the camera was too close, and the table and chair were clipped. Two repair rounds adjusted the framing, hidden front-room extent and furniture proportions. I inspected source, lateral, reverse and textile views before final baking.

Five full/ambient bake groups took 193.17 seconds, using a base resolution of 1024 and 2048 for textiles and outdoor geometry, 32 samples and OpenImageDenoise. A 1024×512 reflection probe took another 6.61 seconds. These are measured stages, not a complete setup or generation stopwatch.

The UV/color/coordinate round trip reported zero error. A separate matched 256×192 browser calibration fixture had a mean absolute RGB difference of 0.003818 on a 0–1 scale against the native expected render. That checks lightmap transport, not resemblance to the source sofa.

Three deliverables with different contracts

Product File bytes What it preserves
Packed Blender master 1,037,640 Editable geometry, cameras, lights and packed PBR source maps
Runtime GLB 2,669,308 Geometry and bindings for the full viewer, with required sidecars
Five EXRs plus reflection probe 92,429,949 Baked lighting and reflections required by that runtime
Runtime model plus those sidecars 95,099,257 Declared file total, before reference image and viewer code
Static portable GLB 8,804,144 Embedded baked appearance for independent glTF consumers

These are decimal MB and file-byte totals, not a measured cold network transfer. The online static preview loads the unchanged portable GLB only after an explicit button press. It does not load the 95 MB runtime set.

Fresh Blender processes reopened the master and independently imported the portable model, then rendered each. Both final GLBs passed the Khronos validator with zero errors and zero warnings. The full viewer's actual downloads matched the final master and portable file hashes.

The portable model embeds five static images and uses unlit materials for its baked appearance. Close surface detail is softer than the native/runtime PBR version. It does not carry the current browser fabric finish, live curtain state or dynamic relighting. The GLB export notes cover a separate optimization workflow; I did not run that pass here or invent before-and-after numbers.

Loading it in the actual Digital Garden renderer

I loaded the portable GLB through the existing Digital Garden Experience and real plant assets, using a local test entry, an inspection camera and derived placement. The garden used Three.js 0.186.1; the original PBR room viewer used 0.180.0. The room imported at scale 1, upright, without an extra rotation.

Path Observed conditions Result
Full WebGL2 room viewer 1340×748 drawing buffer, wind enabled, preset views 601 rendered frames in 10.0066 s, about 60.06 FPS
Garden WebGPU 1265×540, DPR 1, low quality, spring/day, 162,420 plants 600 intervals over 10 s, about 59.99 FPS
Garden WebGL2 fallback Same scene and dimensions About 59.99 FPS; median 16.7 ms, p95 16.8 ms

Both garden paths hit the display's roughly 60 Hz ceiling. This does not show which backend is faster. The sampled garden view reported 175 draw calls and about 12.15 million rendered triangles, including rendering passes. For a controlled submission comparison, use the separate plant instancing benchmark.

The import exposed a placement problem: existing plants intersected the room. I preserved the scatter. A production installation needs a reserved footprint. The live garden has not been changed to include this experimental room. Its portable baked light also cannot follow the garden's sun.

Cloth, hems and the lifecycle bug

The desktop follow-up tested low, middle and high fabric points and the lower hem on both panels: eight bidirectional drag/release cases, plus two pinned upper-hem checks. The ray-hit data actually identified part=hem; cloth hits were not relabelled as hem results. The far lower hem was initially obscured by the sofa, so I navigated into a clear viewing position instead of weakening occlusion checks.

The saved hem-grab capture shows the full cloth viewer during the test. The online portable preview has static curtains.

A separate vertical pull kept rail coverage at zero while moving the middle probe 76.37 mm, a higher probe 5.09 mm, and the pinned top 0 mm. The maximum observed movable held-point error was 3.86 mm, below the stated 5 mm test threshold. Camera transforms/projection and UV0/UV1 fingerprints stayed unchanged. Rendered world vertices matched the solver within Float32 precision.

Native pointer-capture loss, release outside the canvas, trusted browser blur, Source-mode changes, real offscreen pause, wind-off sleep, page exit and return all passed. Real navigation produced pagehide and hidden events and removed the old canvas. Isolated hidden-pause used a restored temporary getter/event because inactive tabs in the in-app browser stayed visible. Extra-touch/cancellation handlers used DOM PointerEvents. Neither simulation is physical-phone evidence.

The tests found a real lifecycle bug: a late context-loss event on a detached old canvas could put its replacement viewer into an error state. I removed the old keyboard/context listeners during disposal and guarded the context handler by session ownership. Dispatching the same old-canvas events after repair left the new viewer ready and its camera unchanged.

Actual WebGL loss, a blocked manifest request and a blocked atlas request each recovered through Retry load. The eight review stages and all three blocking gates passed after repair. The gates check ordering and bytes; the browser observations establish the scoped behavior.

What I would use it for

The editable project is useful as a starting point for an approximate room, especially when I want a builder and Blender scene to continue editing. Review and repair remain part of the work. The geometric artwork, upholstery, wood, stone, outdoor trees and lighting are visibly simplified.

Before using this room as a production garden asset, I would improve the reconstruction, reserve its footprint, reduce the runtime payload and complete real-device checks. The 390×844 layout emulation had no horizontal overflow, but no physical phone was connected. There is also no complete setup timer or per-run token/cost baseline.

Does img2interior work with Codex?

It did in this Windows test, using a new builder, render iterations, local compatibility changes and a viewer repair. This does not establish untouched first-pass reliability across other images or fresh host installations.

Which GLB should I put in another Three.js scene?

The portable file is the self-contained static-appearance export. The runtime GLB requires its declared lightmaps, probe and viewer integration. The packed Blender master is the editing source.

Is it open source?

The tested package is source-available under the img2 Interior Free Use, Restricted Commercialization License 1.0, not an OSI open-source license. Read its output/runtime and third-party terms for your use. This test does not relicense the reference image or toolkit.

Related: Three.js garden rendering guide, Codex machine-skill test and the official img2interior project.

Read the original article, supporting data and updates.

articles.title: GCS Write Errors Ran for 12.5 Hours in us-central1. Spool Uploads to Disk, Drain Later
articles.description: Google's Oct 8 GCS incident listed no workaround. Build a bounded on-disk upload spool in Node that fills during an outage and drains with jitter.
articles.body_html:
• Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 8, 2026, Google Cloud Storage in us-central1 spent twelve and a half hours returning errors and timeouts on writes. Google's incident report puts the impact from 04:00 to 16:30 US/Pacific, which is 11:00 to 23:30 UTC. Every status update posted during the day carried the same line under Workaround: "None at this time."

Then it came back. The final report adds a second window on October 9, 04:05 to 09:46 Pacific, in the us-central1-b zone, for a total of 18 hours and 11 minutes.

If your service writes user uploads or exports straight to a bucket in that region, that was up to 18 hours in which any write could come back as a 503 or hang until your timeout fired, and the writes that did succeed were slow. Google's load balancer is not yours to fix; what your process does with the bytes when the bucket says no is.

The answer fits in plain Node. Failed writes land in a bounded spool on local disk; a drainer pushes them back with jittered retries once the bucket recovers; a gauge shows how deep the backlog is. It all runs against a fake bucket you can break on command, so you can watch the spool fill and empty.

What the report says, and why your client's retries run out

The report is specific. A "traffic sorting optimization configuration update" to the Cloud Storage load-balancing layer bypassed capacity-aware routing and pushed write traffic onto low-capacity backend nodes, which ran out of resources. A separate metadata database issue added errors on top. Engineers tried to add emergency capacity, but per the report "this was blocked by systemic regional capacity limits." The October 9 recurrence came from an incomplete rollback of an upload planner feature.

What clients saw: "Customers primarily observed HTTP 503 UNAVAILABLE errors on WriteObject operations and client-side timeouts." Reads were hit less. Other regions were fine.

The official client's answer to a 503 is on the Cloud Storage retry strategy page, which lists 408, 429 and 5xx responses, plus socket timeouts, as retryable, and recommends exponential backoff with jitter. The Node.js defaults on that page: 3 retries, a 1-second initial wait, a multiplier of 2, a 64-second maximum wait, and a 600-second overall deadline. Uploads are only retried automatically when they are idempotent, meaning you passed an ifGenerationMatch precondition.

So the client gives up after three retries, or ten minutes at the very most. Against a twelve-hour outage, in-request retries are a rounding error. Past that point, the bytes have to live somewhere other than the request, and they have to survive a process restart, because over twelve hours you will deploy, scale, or crash at least once.


When the bucket stops accepting writes, the bytes need a place to wait that outlives the request.

A bounded spool on disk

The spool is a directory. One file per pending object. Each file holds a one-line JSON header with the object name, then the raw bytes. Three rules keep it honest:

  • Write to a temp file, then rename. A crash mid-write leaves a .tmp file that init() deletes, never a half-written entry the drainer would choke on.
  • Cap both file count and bytes. A spool without a cap turns a storage outage into a full-disk outage on your own host.
  • Reserve capacity before the first await. Twenty concurrent failures must not all pass the cap check and then all write. 
// spool.mjs
import {
  mkdir, readdir, readFile, rename, rm, stat, writeFile,
} from 'node:fs/promises';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

export class SpoolFullError extends Error {}

export class Spool {
  constructor(dir, { maxBytes, maxFiles }) {
    this.dir = dir;
    this.maxBytes = maxBytes;
    this.maxFiles = maxFiles;
    this.bytes = 0;
    this.files = 0;
  }

  async init() {
    await mkdir(this.dir, { recursive: true });
    for (const f of await readdir(this.dir)) {
      const path = join(this.dir, f);
      if (f.endsWith('.tmp')) {
        await rm(path, { force: true });
      } else if (f.endsWith('.spool')) {
        this.bytes += (await stat(path)).size;
        this.files += 1;
      }
    }
  }

  async put(name, data) {
    const head = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ name }) + '\n');
    const body = Buffer.concat([head, data]);
    if (this.files + 1 > this.maxFiles ||
        this.bytes + body.length > this.maxBytes) {
      throw new SpoolFullError(`spool full: ${this.files}`);
    }
    // reserve first, so concurrent puts respect the cap
    this.files += 1;
    this.bytes += body.length;
    const id = `${Date.now()}-${randomUUID()}`;
    const final = join(this.dir, `${id}.spool`);
    const tmp = `${final}.tmp`;
    try {
      await writeFile(tmp, body, { flush: true });
      await rename(tmp, final);
    } catch (err) {
      this.files -= 1;
      this.bytes -= body.length;
      await rm(tmp, { force: true });
      throw err;
    }
  }

  async list() {
    const names = await readdir(this.dir);
    return names.filter((f) => f.endsWith('.spool')).sort();
  }

  async oldestAgeMs() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    return first ? Date.now() - Number(first.split('-')[0]) : 0;
  }

  async oldest() {
    const [first] = await this.list();
    if (!first) return null;
    const path = join(this.dir, first);
    const buf = await readFile(path);
    const nl = buf.indexOf(10); // the header ends at the first \n
    const { name } = JSON.parse(buf.subarray(0, nl).toString());
    const data = buf.subarray(nl + 1);
    return { path, name, data, size: buf.length };
  }

  async remove(entry) {
    await rm(entry.path);
    this.files -= 1;
    this.bytes -= entry.size;
  }
}

flush: true makes writeFile call sync() on the handle before closing it, so the bytes are on disk before the rename publishes the entry. The option landed in Node v21.0.0 and v20.10.0 per the Node fs docs. File names start with Date.now(), so a lexical sort gives you oldest-first, and the age of the oldest entry falls out of the name without opening the file. JSON.stringify escapes newlines inside the object name, so the first raw \n in the file always ends the header.

The upload path is short. Try the bucket with a timeout. If the failure is one a retry could fix, spool it. If the spool is full, put throws SpoolFullError and your caller decides what to do, which is the backpressure: return a 503 to your own client, pause a consumer, stop reading from a queue. The one thing you must not do is drop the write silently.

// uploader.mjs
const WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS = 2_000;
const NET = ['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'EPIPE'];

export function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err?.name === 'TimeoutError') return true;
  if (NET.includes(err?.code)) return true;
  const status = Number(err?.code);
  return status === 408 || status === 429 || status >= 500;
}

export async function upload(bucket, spool, name, data) {
  try {
    await bucket.write(name, data, {
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS),
    });
    return 'stored';
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
    await spool.put(name, data); // may throw SpoolFullError
    return 'spooled';
  }
}

The retryable set mirrors Google's list: 408, 429, 5xx, and timeouts. A 403 or 404 is a bug in your code or config, and spooling it would hide that bug for hours. AbortSignal.timeout() gives you a signal that aborts after the given milliseconds with a TimeoutError as its reason, which is what isRetryable checks for.

Drain with full jitter

The drainer is one loop. Take the oldest entry, try to write it, delete it on success. On a retryable failure, sleep a random amount between zero and an exponentially growing ceiling. That is the "full jitter" variant from Marc Brooker's Exponential Backoff and Jitter post on the AWS Architecture Blog. When a region comes back, every client that spooled is about to retry at once. Randomized sleeps spread that herd out instead of hitting the recovering backend in synchronized waves.

// drainer.mjs
import { isRetryable } from './uploader.mjs';

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export async function drain(bucket, spool, opts = {}) {
  const {
    baseMs = 250, capMs = 30_000, idleMs = 1_000,
    timeoutMs = 5_000, signal,
  } = opts;
  let failures = 0;
  while (!signal?.aborted) {
    const entry = await spool.oldest();
    if (!entry) {
      await sleep(idleMs);
      continue;
    }
    try {
      await bucket.write(entry.name, entry.data, {
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
      });
      await spool.remove(entry);
      failures = 0;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isRetryable(err)) throw err;
      failures += 1;
      const ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** failures);
      await sleep(Math.random() * ceiling); // full jitter
    }
  }
}

One drainer per process, writing one entry at a time, is deliberately slow. A recovering storage backend is the worst place to aim a burst. If your backlog is large enough that serial draining takes too long, run a small fixed number of these loops over disjoint entries, not a Promise.all over the whole directory.


Full jitter: each retry waits a random slice of a growing window, so recovering clients don't arrive in lockstep.

The real bucket adapter has one more task beyond calling the client: make the write safe to repeat. A write that timed out on your side may still have landed on Google's side. With ifGenerationMatch: 0, the request preconditions docs say the write only succeeds if no live object with that name exists, and fails with 412 Precondition Failed otherwise. For an object name that is unique per upload, a 412 on a retry means "your earlier attempt worked," so the adapter treats it as success. The preconditionOpts shape is the one Google's Node upload sample uses.

// gcs-bucket.mjs
import { Storage } from '@google-cloud/storage';

function abortable(promise, signal) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
    signal.addEventListener(
      'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
    );
    promise.then(resolve, reject);
  });
}

export class GcsBucket {
  constructor(bucketName) {
    this.bucket = new Storage().bucket(bucketName);
  }

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    const save = this.bucket.file(name).save(data, {
      resumable: false,
      preconditionOpts: { ifGenerationMatch: 0 },
    });
    try {
      await abortable(save, signal);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err?.code === 412) return; // an earlier try landed
      throw err;
    }
  }
}

abortable stops your code from waiting. It does not cancel the HTTP request underneath, which is why the adapter sends the precondition: the abandoned request can still succeed later, and the next attempt has to cope with that. The status-on-err.code check matches how the client's ApiError carries the HTTP status. Confirm it against the client version you pin, because a wrong check here turns every successful retry into a 412 that stops the drainer, with the entry still on disk.

Watch it fill and drain

The fake bucket fails on command. While failing is true, half its writes throw a 503 and the other half hang until the caller's timeout fires, which matches the two symptoms in Google's report.

// fake-bucket.mjs
export class FakeBucket {
  objects = new Map();
  failing = false;

  async write(name, data, { signal }) {
    if (this.failing) {
      if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
        const err = new Error('503 UNAVAILABLE');
        err.code = 503;
        throw err;
      }
      await new Promise((_, reject) => {
        if (signal.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
        signal.addEventListener(
          'abort', () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true },
        );
      });
    }
    this.objects.set(name, Buffer.from(data));
  }
}

The metrics endpoint exposes the three numbers you will alert on, in the Prometheus text exposition format. No client library needed.

// metrics.mjs
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

export function serveMetrics(spool, port = 9464) {
  return createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url !== '/metrics') return res.writeHead(404).end();
    const age = (await spool.oldestAgeMs()) / 1000;
    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/plain; version=0.0.4',
    });
    res.end([
      '# TYPE upload_spool_files gauge',
      `upload_spool_files ${spool.files}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_bytes gauge',
      `upload_spool_bytes ${spool.bytes}`,
      '# TYPE upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds gauge',
      `upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds ${age}`,
      '',
    ].join('\n'));
  }).listen(port);
}

The demo produces 50 writes a second, breaks the bucket from second 2 to second 8, and stops producing at second 10. The spool is capped at 200 files, which a six-second outage at that rate overflows on purpose, so you also see backpressure kick in.

// demo.mjs  (Node 20.10+; run: node demo.mjs)
import { FakeBucket } from './fake-bucket.mjs';
import { Spool, SpoolFullError } from './spool.mjs';
import { upload } from './uploader.mjs';
import { drain } from './drainer.mjs';
import { serveMetrics } from './metrics.mjs';

const bucket = new FakeBucket();
const spool = new Spool('./spool-data', {
  maxBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxFiles: 200,
});
await spool.init();

const stop = new AbortController();
const drainer = drain(bucket, spool, {
  signal: stop.signal, capMs: 2_000,
});
const metrics = serveMetrics(spool);

let n = 0;
const counts = { stored: 0, spooled: 0, rejected: 0 };
const producer = setInterval(async () => {
  const name = `events/${n++}.json`;
  const data = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ n, at: Date.now() }));
  try {
    counts[await upload(bucket, spool, name, data)] += 1;
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof SpoolFullError)) throw err;
    counts.rejected += 1;
  }
}, 20);

const report = setInterval(() => {
  console.log(
    `depth=${spool.files} in_bucket=${bucket.objects.size}`,
    JSON.stringify(counts),
  );
}, 500);

setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = true; }, 2_000);
setTimeout(() => { bucket.failing = false; }, 8_000);
setTimeout(() => clearInterval(producer), 10_000);
setTimeout(async () => {
  stop.abort();
  clearInterval(report);
  metrics.close();
  await drainer;
  console.log('final depth', spool.files);
}, 20_000);

What to look for in the log lines: depth sits at 0 for two seconds, climbs once the bucket breaks, hits the 200 cap, and rejected starts counting. After second 8 the drainer's next attempt succeeds, its failure counter resets, and depth falls back to 0. On a clean run, the number to check at the end is that in_bucket equals stored + spooled: everything the spool accepted made it to the bucket, and everything it refused was reported to the caller, not lost. While it runs, curl localhost:9464/metrics shows the gauges move. Kill the process mid-outage and start it again, and init() picks the backlog up from disk.

Alert on the age, not only the depth. A deep spool that is draining is fine. A shallow spool whose oldest entry is two hours old means the drainer is stuck.

- alert: UploadSpoolStuck
  expr: upload_spool_oldest_age_seconds > 900
  for: 5m
- alert: UploadSpoolNearlyFull
  expr: upload_spool_bytes > 0.8 * 5242880
  for: 2m

Where this stops helping

The spool needs a disk that survives the process. On Cloud Run, the container contract says the writable filesystem "is an in-memory file system, so writing to it uses the instance's memory," and that data written to it "doesn't persist when the instance stops." A spool there eats your memory limit and dies with the instance. Same story for a Kubernetes emptyDir when the pod is deleted. You want a persistent volume, or a VM disk.

Ordering is not preserved. While the spool drains, fresh writes go straight to the bucket and overtake older spooled ones. If a consumer depends on write order, route every write through the spool whenever it is non-empty.

list() reads the whole directory on every drain step. That is fine for thousands of entries and wasteful for millions. At that scale, keep an in-memory index built at init() or move to an append-only log with an offset file.

A poison entry blocks the line. If a spooled object keeps failing with a non-retryable error, the drainer throws and stops, and the age alert above is how you find out. Decide up front whether such entries get moved to a dead-letter directory or need a human.

And the spool lives in the same failure domain as your host. If the zone that holds your disk is the one having a bad day, the backlog waits with it. A second bucket in another region is the other half of this design, and it costs you reconciliation logic on read. The spool buys you hours of not losing data. It doesn't replace that decision.

If this was useful

The spool is a small instance of an old idea: when a dependency is down, absorb the load in a bounded buffer, push back on callers when the buffer fills, and recover gently with jittered retries. The System Design Pocket Guide: Fundamentals covers those building blocks, from queues and backpressure to retries, timeouts and availability trade-offs, so you can reach for the right one before the next status page says "None at this time."
